title: Recipe 34: Evidence relationship labels
body:
Closes #34

## What this adds

`recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels/`: a knowledge-graph relationship labeller. Jev answers
one `Choice` per evidence passage -- which of four fixed relationship types, if any, that single
passage states holds between the two named entities, with `no_supported_relation` as the use
case's own fallback outcome. Python composes these passage-level judgments in two stages
(`helpers.py`): a confidence gate on each passage (`classify_passage`), and a deterministic rule
that composes every passage decision for one entity pair into a single task-level label
(`compose_relation`), sending a pair to an explicit review outcome when any passage was not
confident enough to trust, or when the evidence disagrees about which relationship holds.

The fixtures include the hard case the use case names by name: two tasks, `v01`/`v05-hard`
(`validation`) and `t02`/`t05-hard` (`test`), that each reuse the same two entity names, where one
task's passage states the relationship plainly and the other task's passage, about the same pair,
does not -- so the gold label follows the passage in front of Jev, never the relationship that
holds between the pair elsewhere in this recipe's own fixtures. A second task,
`v11-disagree`/`t11-disagree`, has two evidence passages that confidently name two different real
relationships, which composition sends to review rather than silently preferring one over the
other.

Evaluation reports per-relationship precision, recall and F1 at two granularities: per evidence
passage (`per_class_metrics` against each passage's own gold label) and at the task level
(`per_class_metrics` against each entity pair's own gold label, over the tasks composition
accepted), plus task-level coverage, accuracy and risk via `evaluate_outcomes` (the rule has two
review branches, a confidence gate and a disagreement check, so a bare confidence reconstruction
via `evaluate_selective` does not apply).

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels/`, plus the generated
  README regions regenerated by the integration worker (nothing else outside the recipe folder)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` after updating against current
  `main`, before final review; `--check` passes (it is expected to be red before this
  integration step) -- **not yet done**; this recipe is not yet published, and its builder never
  runs the renderer (see "Decisions" below)
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels/`
  paths, with no symlink, mode or type change, rename or deletion out of scope (checked below;
  `README.md` is untouched by this pull request, so the render-equality part of this box does
  not yet apply)
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definition
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which
  mode it ran in
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases, and carry gold labels
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (`ReviewQueue`, no action log --
  nothing here models an action with an external effect)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels (no baseline named on the issue)
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see "Acceptance criteria" below)

## Acceptance criteria

- Notebook runs top to bottom offline, no key, no network, outputs committed: met -- executed
  twice from a clean kernel, byte-identical.
- Live mode opt-in, same question definitions: met -- `get_backend` reads
  `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE`/`TYPESAFE_API_KEY`; `build_questions()` is the only question definition,
  used by both paths.
- Fixtures synthetic, hard cases, gold labels, pass the validator: met -- `python -m
  jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels` passes; every
  `validation`/`test` row carries a gold label (a dict of the task-level and every passage-level
  label); `v05-hard`/`t05-hard` and `v11-disagree`/`t11-disagree` are the named hard cases.
- Every response fixture records provenance; notebook states its run mode: met -- every stored
  answer's provenance is `synthetic`; the `setup` cell's `run_header` states the mode, and
  `measured` restates it.
- Per-relation F1: met -- `evaluation-per-class` (per question) and `evaluation-task-per-class`
  (task level).
- Deterministic composition is a tested Python function with tests: met --
  `helpers.compose_relation`, tested in `tests/test_helpers.py` (every branch, the branch order,
  and two tests that flip one real, committed stored decision and watch the composed outcome of
  a real fixture, `v08-agree`, change for its own reason).
- Evaluation at task level, not only per question: met -- `evaluation-task-per-class` and
  `evaluation-selective` are both over composed, task-level outcomes.
- No statement about Jev's quality/latency/cost without recorded live inference; synthetic
  metrics labelled pipeline checks: met -- every number is suffixed `{check}`/`{selection}{check}`
  in the offline run this recipe ships.
- README says what it teaches, how to run it, what was/was not measured: met.
- PR changes only the recipe folder, CI green: met except `Catalog (README is current)`, expected
  red until integration (see "Decisions").

## Decisions

- **Granularity.** A "task" is one entity pair with one or more evidence passages; a "scored
  example" (per `docs/fixtures.md`) is the whole task row in `fixtures/inputs.jsonl`, whose
  `replay_keys` lists one key per passage (the same multi-key shape `docs/fixtures.md` already
  documents for an example that makes more than one independent request). Per-question numbers
  are therefore counted over passages (14 `validation`, 14 `test`); task-level numbers are
  counted over tasks (12 `validation`, 12 `test`, four of each bundling two passages). Both
  counts are stated side by side everywhere a number is reported, never compared to each other.
- **The confidence gate is chosen once, at the passage level, from every scored passage in
  `validation`** (not once per task), with `select_confidence_threshold(..., min_coverage=0.85)`
  (pinned, with the keyword, as `helpers.MIN_COVERAGE`, imported by both the notebook and
  `tests/test_helpers.py`). It freezes at `0.6750`.
- **No option is exempt from the gate**, `no_supported_relation` included: every passage decision
  goes through the same confidence check before composition runs. This recipe does not claim the
  CONTRIBUTING.md section 4 exemption for the fallback option; it is simpler to gate every option
  uniformly, and the fixtures include a case (`t12-fallback-wrong`) where a confidently wrong
  `no_supported_relation` is exactly the kind of mistake the gate does not catch, the same as a
  confidently wrong real relationship would be.
- **Composition's two review branches, in order: the confidence gate, then disagreement.** A
  pair with any gated passage goes to review for that reason regardless of what its other
  passages say; only once every passage clears the gate does composition check whether the
  accepted passages agree on a relationship. Because of this second branch, task-level
  coverage/accuracy/risk are reported with `evaluate_outcomes` (the rule's own outcomes), never
  `evaluate_selective` (a bare confidence reconstruction).
- **Entities are fabricated and the "related in the world" fact is established inside this
  recipe's own fixtures, never from a real company or person.** `v01`/`t02` state a real
  relationship for a pair that a different task (`v05-hard`/`t05-hard`) later asks about with a
  passage that does not state it -- a reader can open both committed rows.

## How it was verified

`pip install -e ".[dev]"`, `.venv310` is Python 3.10 with the same extra.

```bash

# recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels: fixtures valid (mode replay)

python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/34-evidence-relationship-labels   # run twice
# 34-evidence-relationship-labels: executed notebook.ipynb offline   (both times; diff empty)

ruff check .
# All checks passed!

ruff format --check .
# 287 files already formatted

python tools/check_hygiene.py
# Hygiene check passed: 414 file(s) scanned.

pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -rX   # both .venv (3.14) and .venv310 (3.10)
# 488 passed, 1 skipped, 34 deselected (both interpreters; no allowlist entry for this recipe)

pytest   # full suite, both interpreters
# 3457 passed, 4 skipped, 34 deselected in 103.41s (3.14) / 124.13s (3.10)

python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base 14fb29e87b55ef7851685bc4f039cbda559a5831 \
  --head fbb98d0d240cc1d7ea0eed4015a6e893809f3bce --branch recipe/34-evidence-relationship-labels \
```

title: Recipe 32: Regression test selection
body:
Closes #32

## What this adds

`recipes/32-regression-test-selection/`: a `Score` recipe that scores candidate tests against the behavior a patch changes, so Python can propose a bounded regression suite under a size budget, built on the pattern of `17-passage-reranking` without reusing its fixtures.

- **Question.** One `Score` per (patch, candidate test) pair, over a four-level rubric Python writes: `unrelated` (0), `same_area` (1), `exercises_change` (2), `direct_regression` (3). Each level stands alone (judged against the state, not against its neighbours).
- **Python's rule** (`helpers.py`): `classify` gates on confidence (`review` below the gate, whatever the level), then applies a fixed `BUSINESS_CUTOFF` (2) to a trusted answer's modal level (`not_relevant` / `relevant`). `propose_suite` composes several `classify` outcomes into one bounded suite: only `relevant`-classified candidates are eligible, ranked by expected `score`, ties broken by baseline rank, truncated at `SUITE_BUDGET` (2) — both constants, not learned from data.
- **Baseline** (required by the issue, since one is named): `baseline_score` = a weighted file-path-overlap signal (does the candidate live in the same feature area as a changed file?) plus `lexical_score` (shared non-stopword words between the patch description and the candidate). One patch (`discount-engine`, both splits) is written so the lexical half is defeated on purpose.
- **Evaluation.** Per-candidate: exact agreement and mean absolute error against the rubric (`validation` and `test`), then selective prediction (`evaluate_selective` / `evaluate_outcomes`, shown to agree — this rule's only review branch is the confidence gate). Task level: `recall_at_budget` / `mean_recall_at_budget` (`jev_cookbook.evaluation`, not hand-rolled) report, per patch and averaged across all 19 patches per split, the recall of each patch's gold-relevant candidates within the proposed suite, against the baseline's own ranking — both "per question" (per patch) and "task level" (the mean).
- **Load-bearing proof.** Two counterfactual cells (and `tests/test_helpers.py`) delete the confidence gate and the size budget in turn and recompute mean recall on real fixtures: both changes move the number on both splits, and `tests/test_helpers.py::test_the_confidence_gate_catches_a_real_review_task_but_the_budget_catches_a_different_one` proves the two bind on disjoint patches.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/32-regression-test-selection/` (the generated README regions are for the integration worker, not this PR)
- [ ] README regenerated — **not applicable to this PR**; per CONTRIBUTING.md's generated-README exception, a separate integration worker regenerates it inside this same PR after handover. `Catalog (README is current)` is expected red until then.
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/32-regression-test-selection/` paths, mode `100644` throughout, no symlink/type change, no rename or deletion out of scope (`tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD` passes, see below)
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network
- [x] Live path is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` + `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MODEL`) and uses the same question definitions
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which mode it ran in (`run_header`, "What was and was not measured")
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference — this recipe has no recorded fixtures, and every metric is labelled a pipeline check
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases (paraphrase that defeats the lexical baseline, a confidently-wrong "claims full coverage" candidate, a low-confidence correct candidate), and carry gold labels
- [x] Python owns every side effect — this recipe simulates no side effect at all (a suite proposal is not an action, nothing is sent, moved, or changed)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, with the baseline the issue names (file-path and lexical overlap)
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (detail below)

## How it was verified

All commands run from the recipe's worktree, in a `uv`-managed venv per `CONTRIBUTING.md`/`docs/recipe-template.md` (Python 3.14 with `.[dev,ml]` for notebook execution and lint, Python 3.10 with `.[dev]` for the floor):

```
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/32-regression-test-selection
  -> recipes/32-regression-test-selection: fixtures valid (mode replay)

python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/32-regression-test-selection   (run twice, 3.14, exact pinned stack)
  -> byte-identical both times (git diff empty)

pytest recipes/32-regression-test-selection   (3.14 and 3.10)
  -> 45 passed (both interpreters)

pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -rX -k "32-regression"   (3.14 and 3.10)
  -> 14 passed, no allowlist entry (both interpreters)

ruff check . && ruff format --check .
  -> All checks passed / 269 files already formatted

python tools/check_hygiene.py
  -> Hygiene check passed: 387 file(s) scanned

python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD --branch recipe/32-regression-test-selection --body-file <this body> --github-repo Jev-Engineering/cookbook
  -> scope ok: recipe pull request for #32 (32-regression-test-selection): 9 changed paths

pytest -q   (full suite, 3.14 and 3.10, one at a time under the shared heavy-job lock)
  -> 3282 passed, 4 skipped, 31 deselected (both interpreters)

python build_fixtures.py   (3.14 and 3.10)
  -> byte-identical inputs.jsonl / labels.jsonl / responses.json on both interpreters
```

## Decisions

- **Rubric and cutoff.** Four levels (`unrelated`/`same_area`/`exercises_change`/`direct_regression`); `BUSINESS_CUTOFF = 2` is a fixed editorial constant, not learned.
- **Confidence gate objective.** Chosen with `select_confidence_threshold(..., min_coverage=0.8)` (not `target_accuracy=1.0`), freezing to `0.4800` on this recipe's `validation` fixtures — a real choice, since several `validation` candidates are wrong at low confidence. `tests/test_helpers.py::test_the_confidence_gate_is_selected_with_min_coverage_not_target_accuracy` pins both the objective keyword and the `0.8` parameter, and a dedicated test greps the notebook source for `min_coverage=0.8` / absence of `target_accuracy`.
- **Size budget.** `SUITE_BUDGET = 2`, a fixed editorial constant (how many proposed tests a reviewer has time for), never searched.
- **Reproducing `propose_suite` through `recall_at_budget` exactly.** `recall_at_budget` always fills its budget from the whole list by score; it has no notion of "eligible", so if a task has fewer eligible candidates than the budget, it would reach into the excluded candidates (tied at a sentinel score) for the remaining slot(s) and award fractional credit `propose_suite` itself never gives. `helpers.effective_budget` closes this by capping the budget passed to `recall_at_budget` at the number of eligible candidates for that specific task; `tests/test_helpers.py::test_effective_budget_and_effective_scores_reproduce_propose_suite_on_a_fixture_shaped_case` demonstrates the bug this fixes and the fix, directly. `helpers.EXCLUDED_SCORE` (`-1.0`, finite — `recall_at_budget` rejects infinities) is the disclosed stand-in score for an excluded candidate.
- **Fixture cohort.** 19 scored patches per split (160 scored candidates total), matching this repository's other Level 3 recipes' measured cohort, rather than a handful of tasks. Three task shapes ("easy", "budget", "gate") make the confidence gate and the size budget each independently, demonstrably load-bearing for the reported recall — proven by literally removing each in the notebook (and in tests) and recomputing.
- **Live request count.** 163, not the full 166-row fixture count: three of the six original `demo` candidates were never decided anywhere in the notebook, so I trimmed the two `demo` tasks down to exactly the three candidates "One answer up close" actually shows (confirmed against `len(answered)` printed at the end of the notebook) rather than let the README/intro overstate the real request count.
- **Baseline weighting.** `baseline_score` = `2 * file_path_score + lexical_score` (file-area match weighted above a single shared word); `discount-engine`'s candidates are written to make the baseline's lexical half fail on purpose, and the task-level evaluation shows the baseline's mean recall is slightly *above* the gated Jev figure overall (it never pays the gate's own coverage cost) — reported plainly, not claimed as a real comparison.
- **Next-steps neighbours.** `17-passage-reranking` and `03-response-clarity-scoring`, both published on `main`.

## Bug I found and fixed mid-build

`recall_at_budget` cannot express "fewer than the budget was proposed" — it always fills its budget by score from the whole list, so my first pass fed it `effective_scores` (a disclosed stand-in score for excluded candidates) with the *raw* `SUITE_BUDGET`. On a task with only one eligible candidate and `SUITE_BUDGET = 2`, this silently credited the second slot to whichever excluded candidate tied for the next-highest (stand-in) score — sometimes the very candidate the confidence gate was supposed to exclude — giving a recall number `propose_suite` itself would never produce (0.6667 where `propose_suite`'s own pick gives 0.5). `helpers.effective_budget` fixes this by capping the budget at the number of actually-eligible candidates per task. I caught it by writing `tests/test_helpers.py::test_recall_at_budget_agrees_with_propose_suite_on_every_task_in_both_splits` (recall must equal `propose_suite`'s own pick, on every one of the 38 scored patches) before trusting any task-level number, and it failed on the "gate" patches until this fix.

## Unfinished / none

Nothing is unfinished. `Catalog (README is current)` is expected red until the integration worker regenerates the root README inside this PR, per CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: Recipe 31: Patch risk triage
body:
Closes #31

## What this adds

Recipe 31, "Patch risk triage" (`recipes/31-patch-risk-triage/`): a Level 3 `Noul` recipe that assesses a small, fabricated patch for three independent concerns -- authentication, input validation, and data loss -- sent together in one request, and composes the three answers into one of three review priorities (`urgent`, `elevated`, `routine`) or an explicit `review` outcome, in a single tested function (`helpers.review_priority`). Builds on #25 (Change evidence review): the same three-independent-`Noul` composition shape, with new fixtures (fabricated patches, not change-ticket narratives) and a different composition (an asymmetric review-priority rule rather than a ready/gaps checklist).

**This recipe prioritises which patches a human reviewer looks at first. It is not a security scanner.** That sentence appears in the notebook's intro, in "Python's part," and again in "What was and was not measured," not only in the README.

### Fixtures: all eight combinations, not four

The issue's three propositions (authentication, input validation, data loss) get the honest extension of the "four combinations" pattern used for two propositions elsewhere: **eight** combinations -- each concern alone (3), each pair (3), all three at once (1), and none (1) -- two patches per combination, split across `validation` and `test` (16 per split), plus three lookalikes per split (one per concern: a patch that genuinely has that one concern, described next to a reassuring, specific-sounding comment -- a ticket number, a claim that a gateway or the platform already handles it -- that the diff itself does not actually show), plus two `demo` patches. 19 validation + 19 test + 2 demo = 40.

| auth | input-validation | data-loss | validation ids | test ids |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F | F | F | v01, v02 | t01, t02 |
| T | F | F | v03, v04 | t03, t04 |
| F | T | F | v05, v06 | t05, t06 |
| F | F | T | v07, v08 | t07, t08 |
| T | T | F | v09, v10 | t09, t10 |
| T | F | T | v11, v12 | t11, t12 |
| F | T | T | v13, v14 | t13, t14 |
| T | T | T | v15, v16 | t15, t16 |
| lookalike (auth=T, rest F) | | | v17 | t17 |
| lookalike (input=T, rest F) | | | v18 | t18 |
| lookalike (dataloss=T, rest F) | | | v19 | t19 |

Every proposition's gold value is authored independently from a separately-written patch, never derived from another proposition's value (CONTRIBUTING.md section 5's "no concern" case is the FFF row).

### Independently consequential, proved on real fixtures

`tests/test_helpers.py` has three tests, each flipping exactly one stored decision on a different real, committed `test` fixture, holding the other two answers fixed:

- `test_authentication_concern_is_independently_consequential_on_the_fixtures` (`t17`: routine -> elevated)
- `test_input_validation_concern_is_independently_consequential_on_the_fixtures` (`t18`: routine -> elevated)
- `test_data_loss_concern_is_independently_consequential_on_the_fixtures` (`t19`: routine -> urgent, not elevated -- this recipe's rule treats a data-loss concern as urgent on its own)

Each test's assertion follows from the one flip it makes and no other; none shares an axis with another.

### Decision design

- `AUTHENTICATION_CONCERN`, `INPUT_VALIDATION_CONCERN`, `DATA_LOSS_CONCERN`: three `Noul` propositions over one patch, sent in one request.
- Per-concern business threshold chosen by F1 on `validation` (`helpers.choose_label_threshold`, pinning `objective="f1"`).
- One confidence gate shared across all three, chosen on their pooled decisions by `min_coverage=` (`helpers.choose_gate`, `helpers.MIN_COVERAGE = 0.8`), **not** `target_accuracy=1.0` -- a 1.0 target forces validation accuracy to 1.0 by construction, which this recipe does not want to report. Both the objective keyword and the constant are asserted by `inspect.getsource` in `tests/test_helpers.py` (`test_choose_label_threshold_selects_by_f1`, `test_choose_gate_selects_by_min_coverage_not_target_accuracy`), and the committed notebook's own printed threshold/gate values are checked against an independently-recomputed value in `test_the_committed_notebook_freezes_the_threshold_and_gate_this_recipe_selects`.
- `helpers.priority_from_concerns(flagged)`: the one explicit rule. A data-loss concern alone, or authentication together with input validation, is `urgent`; exactly one of authentication/input-validation alone (no data loss) is `elevated`; none flagged is `routine`. Any label gated by the confidence gate overrides to `review`.
- Selective metrics for the composed priority come from `evaluate_outcomes` (the review branch is "any of three labels gated," not a single confidence-only rule for the composed outcome); the per-label pooled confidence-only view (`evaluate_selective`/`pool_label_decisions`/`pool_label_outcomes`) is shown separately and the notebook shows the two agreeing (the gate is this rule's only review branch at the per-label level).

### Guard interaction (confidence-gate reason string)

`tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_the_confidence_gate_reason_string_is_exact` requires the literal string `"confidence below the threshold"` in every recipe's `helpers.py`. `Noul` has no confidence field, so this recipe follows the precedent in recipes 25 and 26: the string is `REASON_REVIEW`, the reason `review_priority` actually returns whenever any label is gated (`helpers.decide_concerns`'s `confidence < confidence_gate` check) -- a live branch, never a dead comment. `tests/test_helpers.py::test_review_priority_reviews_whenever_any_label_is_gated` asserts the string comes from that real branch.

### Fixture counts, thresholds, evaluation numbers

- Fixtures: 19 validation, 19 test, 2 demo (40 total), all synthetic, provenance `synthetic`.
- Thresholds (chosen on validation, F1): `authentication_concern` 0.580, `input_validation_concern` 0.500, `data_loss_concern` 0.610.
- Confidence gate (chosen on validation, `min_coverage=0.8`): 0.680.
- Validation: coverage 0.7368, accuracy among answered 0.7857, risk among answered **0.2143** (non-zero).
- Test: coverage 0.8421, accuracy among answered 0.8125, risk among answered **0.1875** (non-zero); review priority matches gold exactly on 0.8125 of the 16 answered patches.
- Per-concern test: all three read precision 1.0000, recall 0.8889, F1 0.9412 (one miss each -- its own lookalike).
- Validation `input_validation_concern` precision is 0.8889 (not 1.0000): a deliberately wrong, low-confidence stored answer (`v02`) is a false positive the business rule alone does not catch.

### Request count (per patch, not per concern)

Counted by instrumenting `backend.decide` (wrapping it with a call counter and replaying the notebook's exact sequence of `decide()` calls): **40** real calls, one per patch (3 concerns per request), for 40 fixtures -- matches `len(fixtures/responses.json)`. README's live section states this and sets the budget guidance to `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=40`.

### Public names introduced

title: Recipe 28: Skill selection
body:
Closes #28

## What this adds

`recipes/28-skill-selection/`: a Level 3 `Score` recipe that scores retrieved skill descriptions for relevance to a task, so Python can select one skill or ask for clarification.

Python retrieves candidates with `helpers.retrieve_candidates` (never hand-picked) and asks one `Score` named `relevance` per `(task, candidate skill)` pair, over a four-level rubric whose levels are described in words, in order. `helpers.select_skill` then composes the result with **two** checks, in this order:

- **the business cutoff** — the top skill's modal level must reach `BUSINESS_CUTOFF` (`suitable`), otherwise the task goes to review;
- **the margin** — the top skill must beat the runner-up by at least the frozen `margin_threshold` (`0.4033333333333334`, chosen on `validation` with `min_coverage=0.5`), otherwise the task goes to review.

All mapping, weighting and arithmetic on scores happens in Python. `Judgment` carries `skill_id`, `level` and `score` — **not** confidence — so the rule cannot read an answer's own confidence even in principle.

## This recipe deliberately has no confidence gate, and that is the decision to read first

An earlier draft added one as a third branch. It was **removed**, on measured grounds, and the removal was upheld by **two independent reviewers**.

The reason, stated as the measurement rather than as arithmetic: `select_confidence_threshold` on this rule's own auto-selected validation pool returns **0.19** — the lowest observed confidence — and a gate there sends **0 of 20** validation and **0 of 20** test auto-selected tasks to review. A reviewer swept it across 32 pool-and-objective combinations and reports it never returning a usable gate; a second reviewer independently verified ten of those, all consistent. `target_accuracy=1.0` raises `ValueError` on this pool. So a house-conforming confidence gate here is a **dead branch**, which this recipe's own independence tests reject. The choice was never "two branches or three" — it was two consequential branches against two plus a dead one.

The notebook prints that measurement (`confidence-gate` cell) rather than asserting it: auto-selected confidence ranges `0.19`–`0.78`; the one wrong auto-selection on each split sits at `0.78`; a correct selection is tied with it at `0.78`; and the gate the house objective would choose is `0.19`, newly reviewing nothing.

**A later builder should not read this as "a `Score` rule with a margin needs no confidence gate."** The transferable question is narrower: *would a gate chosen by `select_confidence_threshold` on my own validation pool change any committed outcome?* Here it would not. Elsewhere it may.

Note that `tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_the_confidence_gate_reason_string_is_exact` requires the literal reason string in every recipe's `helpers.py`. `docs/glossary.md`'s rule is conditional — it governs the reason string **for a confidence-gated review** — so a recipe without such a review breaches nothing in the lexicon, while that check is unconditional. The gap is tracked as a foundation issue; a recipe pull request may not touch the guard or the allowlist.

## Fixtures

**150 `(task, skill)` rows across 50 tasks**: 24 validation tasks (72 rows), 23 test tasks (69 rows), 3 demo tasks (9 rows). Three candidates per task against a fixed five-skill catalog. Every row's answer is stored, so a live run makes **150** requests, one per `(task, skill)` pair — the README's budget note and `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` state 150.

Hard cases, each measured rather than described from memory:

- **A cutoff failure with every retrieved skill only `related`** — `v03`/`t03`, where all three candidates carry gold level 1.
- **A cutoff failure with a clear top candidate that still misses the bar** — `v23`/`t22`, where the top is `related` (level 1) and the other two are `not_suitable` (level 0). That gap is what gives these tasks margin `0.4700`, and it is the reason the business cutoff is **independently** consequential: a task can clear the margin comfortably and still be rejected on level alone.
- **Two skills equally plausible** — `v04`/`t04`.
- **A deliberately wrong pair** — `v22`/`t05`, where a look-alike outscores the skill that fits. Both wrong auto-selections sit at `0.78`, the **highest confidence among auto-selected top answers** — not the highest in the fixtures, which is `0.92`, held by five answers that the rule never auto-selects. That distinction is what makes the dead-gate measurement decisive rather than incidental, and stating it unqualified weakens the case rather than strengthening it.

## Evaluation

Per question — validation: exact-level agreement `0.9444`, mean absolute error `0.5171` levels. Test: `0.9710` and `0.4933`.

Per task — validation: 20 of 24 selected automatically, top-1 accuracy `0.9500`, clarification rate `0.1667`. Test: 20 of 23 selected, top-1 accuracy `0.9500`, **risk `0.0500`**, clarification rate `0.1304`.

Validation accuracy is `0.9500` rather than `1.0000` because `v22` is a wrong, unreviewed, high-confidence validation selection — which is the load-bearing fact of the section above, and is why the figure is falsifiable rather than construction-perfect.

A perfect-accuracy objective is **infeasible** on this pool, not merely a weaker choice: the joint-maximum margin `0.7800` is held by one safe example (`v01`) and one unsafe one (`v22`), so no non-empty answered set is error-free. Maximum attainable accuracy is `0.9500`; `select_confidence_threshold(..., target_accuracy=1.0)` raises. That is pinned by `test_perfect_validation_accuracy_is_infeasible_on_the_margin_pool`, which asserts both the structural cause and the `ValueError`, so a fixture edit that made a perfect threshold reachable fails the test rather than quietly staling the comment.

## Decisions a later builder should know about

- **There is one selection pool, with a filter and a separate safety notion — not two pools.** `pool_for_margin_selection` is the only pool function, and its one filter restricts it to validation tasks whose top skill already clears the business cutoff, because a task the cutoff already rejects cannot inform where the margin should sit. Distinctly from that filter, `is_safe_auto_answer` marks tied tasks unsafe **for threshold selection only**, never for the rule itself. The earlier three-branch design did have two pools; this sentence previously described that design.
- **Both branches are independently consequential, proved by source-level deletion — and the two branches show it differently, which is worth stating precisely.** Deleting the business cutoff moves coverage **and** accuracy on **both** splits, in the same direction each time and with **no new error**: validation 20 of 24 → 21 of 24 with accuracy `0.9500` → `0.9524` and the wrong set still `['v22']`; test 20 of 23 → 21 of 23, `0.9500` → `0.9524`, risk `0.0500` → `0.0476`, wrong still `['t05']`. That uniformity is itself the point, and the reason is a real property of this recipe: the pick the cutoff holds back on `v23`/`t22` is gold level 1 against two gold-level-0 siblings, so it **is** the best of what was retrieved and counts as *correct* under top-1. **The cutoff's value is therefore not that it prevents a wrong top-1 pick — it is that it refuses to act when nothing retrieved is suitable, which top-1 structurally cannot see**, since top-1 only asks whether the best of a bad set was named. That is why the branch's test asserts coverage *and* accuracy change rather than asserting risk rises. Deleting the margin check adds a wrong selection **on validation** — `v05` joins `v22` and accuracy falls `0.9500` → `0.9091` — while **on test** it makes `t04` an unreviewed guess that happens to be **correct**, so coverage rises and accuracy rises with it, to `0.9524`, with the wrong set still exactly `['t05']`. So the margin branch's consequence appears as an added error on one split and as coverage bought without a new error on the other. That is what a margin check does: it trades coverage for safety, and on a given split the trade can come out either way. Each branch's named test fails for its own cause, with no cross-contamination.
- **The scored splits are at the top of the published Level 3 cohort by task-level units**, which is the quantity that matters for task-level metrics. Two different counts are easy to confuse here, so both are stated: this recipe has **72 and 69 scored `(task, skill)` examples** and **24 and 23 task-level units**. Across the published Level 3 recipes, examples per split run roughly 16–81 and units per split run roughly 8–23. By units this recipe is at the top; by examples it is not. The unit count is what lets a top-1 accuracy over 20-odd accepted tasks mean anything — and the two must not be compared against each other, since sizing 20 *examples* at three candidates per task would yield about 7 units, which is the outlier shape this recipe's fixture expansion existed to fix.

## How it was verified

```
pytest recipes/28-skill-selection                              # 46 tests
pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -rX -k 28-skill-selection    # 14 passed, no allowlist entry
pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -rX                          # 474 passed, 1 skipped, 33 deselected
pytest    # full suite, py3.10 [dev]:      3418 passed, 4 skipped, 33 deselected
pytest    # full suite, py3.14 [dev,live]: 3478 passed, 2 skipped, 33 deselected
ruff check . ; ruff format --check .                           # clean
python tools/check_hygiene.py                                  # passed
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate --all                 # all 33 recipes + template
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/28-skill-selection --body-file pr-body.txt      # scope ok
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/28-skill-selection    # twice, clean kernel, byte-identical
```

The notebook commits one figure (`evaluation-curve`, 46,792 base64 characters), unchanged across every round.

The three whole-repository counts above are measured at the final integrated head, where 33 recipes are published. Any whole-repository figure in a description goes stale at the next integration; the recipe-scoped counts are the ones that reproduce unchanged.

## Review history

Six fix rounds and **two independent reviewers**, both required to approve because the no-confidence-gate decision sets a precedent for the recipes still to be built — the same standard applied to changes to the template and the scaffolder.

Four successive justifications for that decision were each found false in a different way: an algebraic one false at the frozen threshold; a measured one wrong in three particulars; an inverted inference about which threshold the house objective would pick, which was a review note and never shipped in the recipe, unlike the other three; and a claim that was **true of the original fixture pool** and falsified by the round that expanded it. Each was caught by asking a reviewer to verify a derivation at the current numbers rather than read it. The surviving argument is printed, test-pinned, or both.

The recipe's own code and fixtures were sound throughout; every one of those failures was in prose or a comment explaining the code.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes confined to `recipes/28-skill-selection/`, plus the generated regions of the root `README.md` added in this pull request's integration stage
- [x] README regenerated by a separate integration worker, never the builder; `render(base README, head catalog)` verified byte-for-byte, marker pairs at identical line numbers, and — against the second merge as baseline — both differing lines strictly inside generated regions (against the first merge's baseline it is three lines, since that baseline predates recipe 32; each count is right for its own baseline)
- [x] `tools/check_recipe_scope.py` passes
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline with no key and no network; outputs committed; byte-identical on re-execution
- [x] Live mode opt-in, sharing the same question definitions
- [x] Every response fixture records provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states its mode
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency or cost; every number labelled a pipeline check
- [x] Fixtures synthetic, hard cases present, gold labels, validator passes
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions simulated
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels at question **and** task level
- [x] `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` passes with **no allowlist entry**

## Acceptance criteria (issue #28)

- [x] Live mode opt-in, same question definitions

- [x] Provenance recorded; notebook states its mode

## Open, and deliberately not fixed here

Two items recorded for a later prose sweep rather than fixed, because fixing them would void two verified approvals whose carry-forward rests on an empty recipe-path diff: a connector in a `build_fixtures.py` comment that implies a fixture is in the margin pool *because* its distribution is spread (the actual filter is the business cutoff — every individual claim in the sentence is true), and the template-boilerplate sentence "every number below carries that mode with it", which is false for the demo answer displays and per-example lines in the template and all published recipes alike.

title: Recipe 33: Schema field mapping
body:
Closes #33

## What this adds

`recipes/33-schema-field-mapping/`: a Level 3 recipe that maps source fields from a fabricated
legacy export to a fixed target schema. Jev answers one `Choice` per source field (its name,
declared type and description) over the eight target-schema fields plus `ambiguous` and
`unmapped`; Python then validates the proposed mapping in two stages
(`helpers.gate_field`, then `helpers.apply_one_to_one`): a declared-type check against the
chosen target, and a one-to-one constraint across each export batch's own fields, with every
conflict reported. Evaluation is at the field level (per question) and at the task (batch)
level, and reports the number of conflicts Python's validation catches.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/33-schema-field-mapping/`, plus the generated README
      regions (not yet regenerated by the integration worker; see below)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` -- not run by this builder
      (CONTRIBUTING.md's generated-README exception); `Catalog (README is current)` is expected
      red until the integration worker runs it
- [x] `git diff --raw -M` against the base lists only `recipes/33-schema-field-mapping/` paths,
      every mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change, no rename or deletion out of scope
      (`tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base a994608156eb7f4da5acba9e0e0be9c47829b672 --head HEAD
      --branch recipe/33-schema-field-mapping --body-file <this file>` reports `scope ok`)
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network; executed twice under
      `tools/execute_notebook.py`, byte-identical both times
- [x] Live path is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`) and uses the same
      `helpers.build_questions()` definition as the offline path
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook's `run_header`
      and "What was and was not measured" section state the mode
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost anywhere; every metric is printed with
      `(a pipeline check, not a Jev result)` offline, and validation numbers additionally carry
      `(a selection step, not a reported result)`
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic (35 fields, 16 `validation` / 16 `test` / 3 `demo`, grouped into 16
      scored export batches of 2 fields each plus one 3-field demo batch), include every hard
      case the issue's Build notes name (misleading field name resolved by its description,
      `ambiguous`, `unmapped`, a one-to-one conflict, a declared-type mismatch), and carry gold
      labels for every scored field
- [x] Python owns every side effect; nothing is applied or executed -- a `review` outcome only
      queues the field, with the model's own answer attached, in a `jev_cookbook.simulation.
      ReviewQueue`
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels at the field level and the task level, with
      `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes` (never `evaluate_selective`: the rule has three
      review branches beyond the confidence gate -- `ambiguous`, a type mismatch, and the
      one-to-one conflict -- so the confidence-only view and the rule's own outcomes can and do
      disagree; the issue names no baseline to compare against)
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below)

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `notebook.ipynb` runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network, and its outputs
      are committed -- executed twice under `tools/execute_notebook.py`, byte-identical.
- [x] Live mode is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`) and uses the same question
      definitions as the offline run (`helpers.build_questions()`, called identically by both
      the notebook's setup cell and `build_fixtures.py`).
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases named in the Build notes (misleading field
      names, `ambiguous`, `unmapped`), carry gold labels, and pass the fixture validator
      (`python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/33-schema-field-mapping` ->
      `fixtures valid (mode replay)`).
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`, enforced by
      `jev_cookbook.DecisionResult`); the notebook states its run mode in the header and in "What
      was and was not measured".
- [x] Evaluation: mapping accuracy (`accuracy(gold, raw_choice)`, both splits) and the number of
      conflicts caught by validation (`helpers.conflict_count`: 2 on `validation`, 2 on `test`).
- [x] The deterministic composition lives in Python functions in `helpers.py`
      (`gate_field`, `apply_one_to_one`, `compose_task`) with tests in `tests/test_helpers.py`
      covering every branch, including two tests that flip only the model's answer or only a
      declared type on a real committed fixture and show the composed outcome changes.
- [x] Evaluation is at task level (`helpers.task_accepted_and_correct`, one row per export batch)
      as well as per question/field (`helpers.field_accepted_and_correct`).
- [x] No statement about Jev's quality, latency, or cost appears anywhere; every metric in a
      synthetic run is labelled a pipeline check (and a selection step, on `validation`).
- [x] `README.md` says what the recipe teaches, how to run it offline and live, and what was and
      was not measured live.
- [x] The pull request changes only `recipes/33-schema-field-mapping/`; CI is green except
      `Catalog (README is current)`, expected red until integration.

## Decisions

- **Target schema and fabricated names.** Eight target fields (`customer_email`, `customer_id`,
  `order_total`, `order_date`, `loyalty_tier`, `shipping_country`, `product_sku`,
  `is_gift_order`) for a fabricated retailer ("Marrowfield Mercantile", named only in a
  `helpers.py` comment); source batches are named generically (`batch_v01`..`batch_v08`,
  `batch_t01`..`batch_t08`, `batch_d01`) rather than as named legacy tables, after an earlier
  draft's domain-pure table names forced an awkward choice between a degenerate one-field task
  and mixing two unrelated domains under one table name; a later builder who wants named tables
  back can rename the task ids without touching anything else, since they are pure Python
  bookkeeping.
- **`ambiguous` is an unconditional deferral; `unmapped` is gated like a real target.**
  `ambiguous` always goes to `review`, whatever its confidence (CONTRIBUTING.md section 4 part
  (a): it asks a person to pick between two real candidates the description does not settle,
  which is a deferral). `unmapped` is a complete answer and would qualify for section 4's
  fallback exemption (no action is ever recorded, and a wrong `unmapped` leaves nothing standing
  beyond the missed field, same as review would), but, like the template's own `none`, this
  recipe still gates it on confidence and checks no declared type against it (there is none to
  check) rather than claim the exemption -- gating a qualifying fallback anyway is compliant.
- **One-to-one conflicts are symmetric.** When two fields in one batch are both accepted into the
  same real target, *both* are sent to review, not one chosen over the other: nothing in either
  field's own answer tells Python which proposal (if either) is right.
- **Threshold objective: `min_coverage=0.85`, not `target_accuracy=1.0`** (rule 12), pinned in
  `tests/test_helpers.py::test_the_frozen_threshold_objective_is_pinned`. The frozen gate is
  `0.7778`.
- **`test_stored_answers_are_not_all_right` is the strong form**: it re-derives the threshold
  inline from `validation` and asserts a `wrong_and_confident` list built with a literal
  `>= threshold` comparison, then separately asserts the full composed-pipeline mistake
  (`t16-wrong`, accepted with the wrong target) -- satisfying `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`'s
  AST-based G1(c) check, which scans this exact function's body for that shape.
- **A bug I found and fixed myself, mid-build (the rule-11 kind of mistake, reported as asked):**
  my first threshold choice (`min_coverage=0.85` with the validation "wrong" field
  `promo_code_applied` stored at a *high* confidence, `0.90`) made `select_confidence_threshold`
  pick the *lowest* observed confidence (`0.3333`) regardless of `min_coverage`, because that
  lone low-confidence point happened to be a *correct* `ambiguous` answer, so excluding it only
  ever hurt validation accuracy -- the confidence gate's `REASON_LOW_CONFIDENCE` branch never
  fired anywhere in the fixture set as a result, which would have shipped a recipe whose
  "confidence gate" demonstration was vacuous. I caught this by printing the full
  `selective_curve` before writing any evaluation prose, and fixed it by lowering
  `promo_code_applied`'s stored confidence to `0.50` so the gate has a real, validation-side
  mistake to exclude, distinct from the one-to-one conflict's catch. Separately, an early
  version of `tests/test_helpers.py::test_stored_answers_are_not_all_right` asserted an exact
  list of "wrong and confident" raw ids that turned out to include `t11-conflict` (a field the
  one-to-one check catches, not the confidence gate) -- the test failed against its own
  intended semantics, which is what led to splitting it into the raw-mistake assertion
  (satisfying the recipe-guard's strong-form check) and a separate, precise assertion on the

title: Recipe 30: Citation verification
body:
Closes #30

## What this adds

`recipes/30-citation-verification/`: a Level 3 `Choice` recipe that checks each answer claim
against its cited passage.

Python resolves a claim's citation (a document id and a section number) against a small, fixed
corpus (`helpers.CORPUS`) before any request is made. A citation that does not resolve is
flagged for correction directly — no `Choice` is ever built for it, since there is nothing for
one to weigh (CONTRIBUTING.md section 3). A citation that does resolve asks one `Choice` named
`relation` (`supported`/`unsupported`/`contradicted`), adapted from TypeSafe's citation-checking
cookbook (S06). `helpers.classify` composes the result: below the frozen confidence gate, a
claim goes to review; at or above it, a confident `supported` claim is kept as cited, and a
confident `unsupported`/`contradicted` claim is flagged for correction.

The two hard cases the issue's build notes name are both in the fixtures and shown up close in
the notebook: a citation that never resolves (`demo-01-no-document`, `v-broken-*`,
`t-broken-*`), and a correct claim that cites the wrong passage (`demo-02-wrong-passage`,
`*-u3/u4/u5-wrongpassage`) — the latter is also where both splits' confidently-wrong answers
live (`v-u3-wrongpassage`, `t-c5-wrong`, `t-u3-wrongpassage`).

Evaluation covers both levels Level 3 asks for:
- **Per-question**: raw `Choice` accuracy and a confusion matrix, over the 16 claims per split
  whose citation resolves.
- **Claim-level (task level)**: `evaluate_outcomes` (coverage/accuracy/risk over all 19 claims
  per split, since an unresolved citation is an unconditional accept outside the confidence
  gate); `helpers.flag_agreement`; and `per_class_metrics` for `supported`/`unsupported`/
  `contradicted` over the full composed verdict — the acceptance criterion's "claim-level F1 for
  the unsupported and contradicted classes".

A trivial "trust every resolved citation" baseline (0.4737 both splits) is reported for
comparison against the raw choice's 0.8750.

## What the model earned, and what Python's bookkeeping contributed

Three claims per split have an unresolved citation, are decided by Python alone without the
model being asked, and are **correct by construction**. Any composed figure therefore includes
three free correct answers. The notebook prints `forced (unresolved citation) claims: 3 of 3,
correct by construction` on both splits and reports a **resolved-only twin beside every
composed figure**, so a reader can see which part the model earned:

| figure (test split) | composed | resolved-only |
|---|---|---|
| accuracy | 0.8889 | 0.8667 |
| risk | 0.1111 | 0.1333 |
| flag agreement | 0.8421 | 0.8125 |
| `unsupported` recall | 0.7500 | 0.6000 |
| `unsupported` F1 | 0.8571 | 0.7500 |

Three of the six `unsupported` true positives are Python's bookkeeping rather than the model's
decision. The recipe's lesson survives this and is in fact sharper for it: measured
resolved-only, the gap between `unsupported` and `contradicted` **widens**, which is the thing
the recipe is teaching. This disclosure was added in review; the figures were recomputed
independently of the review's own table and agree to four decimal places.

## Decisions a later builder will have to live with

- **Three-way `Choice`, not four.** `unsupported` serves double duty as both "the passage says
  nothing" and this use case's own fallback outcome (CONTRIBUTING.md section 3); there is no
  model-facing option for "citation unresolved" — that case never reaches a question at all.
- **`min_coverage=0.75`, not `target_accuracy=1.0`.** Chosen deliberately to avoid adding
  another occurrence of the validation-accuracy-forced-to-1.0 pattern tracked set-wide in #222:
  the frozen threshold (0.4500) is the highest-accuracy point at or above 75% coverage of the
  resolved-citation validation subset, and the resulting validation accuracy (0.9444) and risk
  (0.0556) are genuine outputs of the fixture set, not a search target.
- **The objective is pinned, and by two mechanisms that cover different halves.**
  `helpers.MIN_COVERAGE` and `helpers.resolved_subset` are shared by the notebook and the tests
  rather than restated in each, and a test re-derives the threshold the **committed notebook
  itself printed**. Measured: swapping the objective to `target_accuracy=1.0` *without*
  re-executing leaves the suite green and is caught by CI's notebook-freshness job; *with*
  re-execution the committed-notebook pin fails. Changing `MIN_COVERAGE` alone fails the same
  test. Held jointly, there is no green gap.
- **`evaluate_outcomes`, not `evaluate_selective`, for the whole-split numbers.** An unresolved
  citation is accepted unconditionally (no confidence to gate), so the rule's review branch is
  more than a plain confidence comparison; `select_confidence_threshold` itself is only ever
  given the resolved-citation subset's own confidences.
- **Baseline-accuracy tie is real, not a copy/paste bug.** Both splits' trust-citation-baseline
  accuracy land on 0.4737 because this fixture set gives each split the identical category mix
  (6 supported / 5 contradicted / 5 unsupported / 3 unresolved); the notebook discloses this.
- **Fixture size:** 40 examples (2 demo, 19 validation, 19 test); 33 of the 40 have a citation
  that resolves and so ask the model exactly once each (cached in `decide()`); the other 7 never
  reach a question.

## Fixture generation cannot silently mislabel a stored answer

`build_fixtures.py`'s per-row spec requires an explicit `(top, confidence)` tuple. There is no
default branch: a bare float now raises `TypeError` rather than quietly assigning the positive
label. A test reads the **committed** `fixtures/responses.json` back against `ROWS` and asserts
every stored answer's top choice is the one its own spec names.

This exists because an earlier draft of the generator did default the top choice, which silently
mislabelled the stored answers of rows whose gold label was negative. The rows were corrected,
but for a while the mechanism that produced the error was still in place and nothing tested for
it — reintroducing the original defect on `v-c1` left the fixture validator and the whole suite
green. The test now fails naming the row.

## Independent-consequence proof

`tests/test_helpers.py::test_citation_resolution_is_independently_consequential_on_a_real_fixture`
and `::test_the_models_choice_is_independently_consequential_on_a_real_fixture` each vary **one**
stage on a real committed fixture while holding the other fixed, and assert the composed
verdict/action changes.

Each test fails for its **own** cause and not via the other's, which is the property that makes
them proofs rather than a single proof written twice. Measured on this head: making the model's
`Choice` ineffective fails the model's-choice test and **not** the resolution test; neutering
`resolve_citation` fails the resolution test and **not** the model's-choice test. An earlier
version of both tests varied the same underlying axis and shared an incidental dependency on the
selected threshold, which made each fire for the other's mutation; the tests now fix the gate at
a constant so that coupling is gone. Both mutations are written out inline in the test file, so
the proof travels with the code.

## Live request count

**33** real requests in live mode — one per claim whose citation resolves, each decided once and
reused wherever it is shown again. The 7 unresolved-citation rows never reach a question.
Counted by instrumenting the decide path across every committed code cell, which yields 33 calls
with 33 distinct payloads and zero duplicates; `len(fixtures/responses.json)` agrees but is not
the same quantity, since an unused key or a twice-decided example would break that equality
invisibly. Pinned by
`tests/test_helpers.py::test_every_replay_key_in_the_fixtures_matches_the_current_question`
(empty `replay_keys` for the 7 unresolved rows, exactly one key for the other 33). The README's
budget note states 33 and instructs `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=33`.

## Every number quoted in prose matches the committed output

Every bare metric value in every markdown cell appears in some code cell's committed output in
the same notebook, checked cell by cell after the final re-execution rather than from the run
the prose was drafted against.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/30-citation-verification/`, plus the generated regions of
  the root `README.md` added in this pull request's integration stage
- [x] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` — by a separate integration
  worker, never the recipe's builder, in this same pull request; see the integration receipt
  comment for the byte-for-byte verification that the head README equals
  `render(base README, head catalog)`
- [x] `tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD` passes: 9 changed paths, all
  under `recipes/30-citation-verification/`
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which
  mode it ran in
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases, and carry gold labels
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (`ActionLog`/`ReviewQueue`)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, with a trivial trust-citation baseline for comparison

## Acceptance criteria (issue #30)

- [x] `notebook.ipynb` runs top to bottom offline, outputs committed — executed twice from a
  clean kernel; second run byte-identical to the first.
- [x] Live mode opt-in, same question definitions — `tools/execute_notebook.py` strips
  `JEV_COOKBOOK_*`/`TYPESAFE_*`; the live path calls `helpers.build_questions()` identically.
- [x] Fixtures synthetic, hard cases present, gold labels, pass the validator — validator passes
  in mode `replay`; both named hard cases are present.
- [x] Every response fixture records provenance (`synthetic`); notebook states its mode in
  `run_header` and the "What was and was not measured" cell.
- [x] Claim-level F1 for `unsupported` and `contradicted` — `eval-claimlevel` cell, via
  `per_class_metrics` over the full composed verdict, reported composed and resolved-only.
- [x] Deterministic composition lives in `helpers.classify`, tested in `tests/test_helpers.py`
  (32 tests in the recipe's own suite, including the two independent-consequence proofs, the
  committed-fixture spec check, and the committed-notebook threshold pin).
- [x] Evaluation at task level, not only per question — `evaluate_outcomes` + `flag_agreement`
  + claim-level `per_class_metrics`, alongside the raw per-question accuracy/confusion matrix.
- [x] No Jev quality/latency/cost claim without recorded live inference; synthetic metrics
  labelled `{check}`/`{selection}{check}` throughout.
- [x] README states what it teaches, how to run it, what was/was not measured live.
- [x] Pull request changes only `recipes/30-citation-verification/` (plus the integration
  stage's generated README regions).

## How it was verified

```
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/30-citation-verification   # fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/30-citation-verification                                     # 32 tests
pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -k 30-citation-verification               # 14 passed, no allowlist entry
pytest    # full suite, py3.10 [dev]:        3103 passed, 4 skipped, 28 deselected
pytest    # full suite, py3.14 [dev,live,ml]: 3163 passed, 2 skipped, 28 deselected
ruff check .                                                                # All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                                                       # already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py                                               # passed
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD           # scope ok: 9 changed paths
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/30-citation-verification           # twice, clean kernel; byte-identical
```

The local py3.14 run installs `[dev,live,ml]`; CI's `Tests (py3.14)` leg installs `[dev,live]`
and `Tests (py3.10)` installs `[dev]`. A local run with different extras is not equivalent
coverage in either direction, so both CI legs are the authority and both are green on this head.

The deselected 28 are the wave close-out `catalog_audit` cases, one per published recipe; the
count rises by one when this recipe publishes.

## Review history

Three review rounds, all on this branch:

1. Four must-changes, every one in the test layer rather than in the recipe's outputs: the
   fixture-generation default described above; two independent-consequence tests that did not
   fail for the causes they were named for; an unpinned threshold objective; and the
   undisclosed correct-by-construction subset. The committed fixtures and notebook were sound
   throughout — what was missing was the machinery that would catch them becoming unsound.
2. All four re-verified by mutation, with collected test node ids compared across heads to show
   nothing was lost: removed set empty, added set exactly the new tests. One new must-change
   introduced by that round's own comments.
3. That must-change: five comment lines cited documents outside the repository — a pull request
   description, and house review-brief rule numbering that exists in no committed file. A
   squash merge discards the branch, so a pointer to a pull request body is guaranteed to
   dangle. All of them now state the property the test guarantees instead of naming a rule.
   Citations of committed files (`G1(c)`, which is defined in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` and
   `docs/notebook-ci.md`) were kept.

## Open, and deliberately not fixed here

Two numbers are stated in prose without a printed counterpart in a code cell: a `0.56`
confidence and a count of `15` claims. Both were verified correct in review. They are left as
they are rather than spending a further round on them, and are recorded here so a later reader
knows they were seen rather than missed.

title: Recipe 25: Change evidence review
body:
Closes #25

## What this adds

`recipes/25-change-evidence-review/`: a Level 3 `Noul` recipe that checks whether a proposed
change includes sufficient implementation, validation, and rollback evidence, and composes the
three independent judgments into a deterministic review checklist (`ready`, `gaps` naming
exactly which evidence types are missing, or `review`).

- Three independent `Noul` propositions per change record, asked together in one request:
  `implementation_evidence`, `validation_evidence`, `rollback_evidence` (named with an
  `_evidence` suffix throughout so a proposition is never confused with the `validation`/`test`
  fixture split of the same word).
- `helpers.review_checklist` composes the three label decisions into `ready` / `gaps` / `review`;
  tested for every one of the eight gap combinations and every gating combination in
  `tests/test_helpers.py`.
- Fixtures (40 records: 19 validation, 19 test, 2 demo) cover all eight combinations of the
  three gold propositions, so every pair of propositions is exercised in all four of its own
  combinations (each alone, both together, neither) without a fixture group dedicated to any
  one pair. Three further records (one per proposition, present on both validation and test)
  mention that evidence type without actually supplying it -- the use case's own named hard
  case: a record that mentions a rollback plan without describing one.
- `tests/test_helpers.py` proves each of the three propositions is independently consequential
  on real, committed `test` fixtures (`t03`, `t05`, `t09`): flipping one stored decision, holding
  the other two fixed, changes the composed outcome.
- Evaluation reports precision/recall per proposition (ungated, business rule alone), and at
  task level: `ready`/`gaps`/`review` counts, coverage/accuracy/risk via `evaluate_outcomes`, a
  confusion matrix over the answered subset, and `exact_set_match` for how often the composed
  gap list matches the record's gold combination of evidence types exactly (the use case's own
  "accuracy of the gap list").

## Decisions

- **Label naming.** The three Noul propositions are named `implementation_evidence`,
  `validation_evidence`, `rollback_evidence` (not the shorter `implementation`/`validation`/
  `rollback`) specifically so `validation_evidence` (the proposition) is never confused with the
  `validation` split in prose or code.
- **No fallback/unconditional branch.** The only review path is the shared confidence gate; the
  rule never has a second unconditional branch, so `evaluate_selective` (confidence-only view)
  and `evaluate_outcomes` (the rule's own outcomes, via `pool_label_outcomes`) agree on every
  field but `threshold` on `test` -- printed side by side in `evaluation-pooled` rather than
  asserted, per the recipe-24 review's lesson not to claim a difference that isn't there.
  `evaluate_outcomes`/`evaluate_selective` are reported (not `evaluate_threshold` alone) for the
  task-level numbers because the composed rule's review branch is a three-proposition pooled
  gate, matching the Noul three-path pattern in `docs/evaluation.md`.
  per-proposition precision/recall use `evaluate_threshold`/`threshold_sweep` (ungated, the
  business rule alone), which is the right tool there since each proposition's own business
  rule has no review branch of its own.
- **Task-level gold.** `helpers.gold_gap_set(label)` reads the three gold booleans already in
  `labels.jsonl` and returns the set of insufficient ones; it never derives one proposition's
  gold value from another's. The stored `"outcome"` field in each label record (`ready`/`gaps`)
  is likewise a function of all three independently authored booleans together, not of one
  standing in for another.
- **Representative sweep chart.** Only `rollback_evidence`'s threshold sweep is charted (not all
  three), since it is the proposition the use case's named hard case bears on; all three
  propositions' frozen thresholds and test precision/recall/F1 are printed.
- **Next steps.** Links `02-refund-intent-detection` (`Noul`, same `Workflow & service
  operations` category) and `18-duplicate-incident-matching` (`Choice`, same category), both
  already published on `main`. No link to this recipe exists yet from any other recipe's own
  Next steps -- expected: `next_steps_inbound_links` (`catalog_audit`, deselected by default) is
  a wave close-out check that a new recipe's own pull request can never satisfy (nothing in this
  recipe's own folder can add a backlink from an older, already-merged recipe).

## How it was verified

```bash
python recipes/25-change-evidence-review/build_fixtures.py          # 40 examples, 38 labels, 40 responses
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/25-change-evidence-review   # fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/25-change-evidence-review                              # 38 passed
pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py -k "25-change-evidence-review or _template"  # 25 passed
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/25-change-evidence-review    # twice; byte-identical
ruff check .                                                           # All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                                                  # files already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py                                          # passed, 358 files scanned
pytest                                                                  # full suite, under HEAVY.lock
```

Run twice, in fresh virtual environments matching CI's two legs:

- **py3.10, `pip install -e ".[dev]"`**: `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` / hygiene /
  fixture validator (`--all`) all clean; full `pytest` -> 3099 passed, 4 skipped, 28 deselected.
- **py3.14, `pip install -e ".[dev,live]"`**: same four checks clean; full `pytest` -> 3159
  passed, 2 skipped, 28 deselected (the live extra unlocks more tests, hence the different
  totals).
- `pytest -m catalog_audit tests/test_recipe_guard.py`: 5 failed (24, 25, 26, 27, 29 each have no
  inbound Next-steps link yet), 23 passed, 405 deselected -- expected; this marker is deselected
  from default CI and is a wave close-out audit this recipe's own pull request cannot satisfy
  (see "Decisions" above).
- The notebook was executed offline twice from a clean kernel (`python tools/execute_notebook.py
  recipes/25-change-evidence-review`, under the shared `HEAVY.lock`); the two runs are
  byte-identical.

**Expected red check:** `Catalog (README is current)` -- the root `README.md` is generated and
this recipe's builder never runs `tools/render_catalog.py`; a designated integration worker
regenerates it inside this same pull request per the generated-README exception in
CONTRIBUTING.md.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/25-change-evidence-review/`, plus the generated README
  regions regenerated by the integration worker (nothing else outside the recipe folder)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` after updating against current
  `main`, before final review; `--check` passes (it is expected to be red before this
  integration step) -- **not done by this builder; integration worker's step**
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/25-change-evidence-review/`
  paths, no symlink, mode or type change, rename or deletion out of scope

- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance; the notebook states which mode it ran in
