title: Foundation: stable seeded permutation helper for per-item option order (#181)
body:
Closes #181

Base: `main` @ `3139f472fe383649977f6ed37514b4e3c46706b3` (PR #183, the tip when this branch was cut).

## What this adds

A shared, documented-stable permutation helper for per-item option order, in
`jev_cookbook.fixtures`:

- `stable_permutation(seed_key: str, n: int) -> tuple[int, ...]` — a permutation of
  `range(n)`, deterministic in `seed_key` alone.
- `stable_shuffle(seed_key: str, items: Sequence[T]) -> tuple[T, ...]` — `items` reordered by
  that same permutation.

**Construction, and why:** a hand-written Durstenfeld (Fisher-Yates, swapping from the end)
shuffle, driven only by `random.Random(seed).random()`, where `seed` is the first 64 bits of
the SHA-256 digest of `seed_key` read as an int (the same seeding convention
`ScriptedBackend.rng_for` already uses). I did **not** use `random.Random(...).shuffle()`: I
checked the `random` module's own docs, and they commit only `Random.random()` to producing the
same sequence for the same seed across CPython versions —

> "The generator's `random()` method will continue to produce the same sequence when the
> compatible seeder is given the same seed."

— and make no such promise about `shuffle()` (which draws from `_randbelow()`/`getrandbits()`
instead). Building the shuffle by hand out of nothing but `random()` calls means the result is
pinned by two things that are each independently stable forever: SHA-256 (a fixed
specification) and that one documented method. That is issue #181's "Fisher–Yates driven by
`random.Random(...)`'s `random()` sequence" option; I went with it over an explicit hash-ranked
order because it stays byte-identical to the derivation `ScriptedBackend.rng_for` and recipe
12's existing (soon-to-migrate) local helper already use, rather than introducing a third
convention.

New file: `src/jev_cookbook/fixtures/permutation.py`. Both names are re-exported from
`jev_cookbook.fixtures` and added to its `__all__`; public signatures of everything else are
unchanged.

### Docs

- `docs/fixtures.md`: new "Per-item option order" section telling recipe authors to derive
  per-example shuffles and first-shown sides from `stable_permutation`/`stable_shuffle`, never
  `random.shuffle` or list position, with the two reasons (the `random.shuffle`
  cross-version-stability gap, and list position proxying grouped/authored gold order — recipe
  12's own history is the worked example of the latter).
- `docs/backends.md` ("Scripted backend"): documents the review of `ScriptedBackend.rng_for`'s
  callers asked for in the issue. **Finding: no behaviour change needed.** I grepped every
  `script`/`ScriptedBackend` use in `src/`, `tests/`, and every `recipes/*/helpers.py` — the only
  real caller today is `tests/test_backends.py`'s `script`/`noisy` functions, which already use
  only `rng.random()`; no recipe currently ships a `script` function at all (every recipe so far
  is in replay mode). The existing pinned
  `random.Random(12345).random() == 0.41661987254534116` assertion in
  `test_scripted_is_deterministic_and_seeded` already is the byte-reproduction test for the one
  method this relies on, so per the issue ("document it ... and add a byte-reproduction test
  rather than changing behaviour") there was nothing to change — I added the explicit
  reasoning and the review note to `docs/backends.md` instead, plus a pointer to the new helper
  for any future script that needs a per-item order.

### Tests

New `tests/test_permutation.py`:

- Pinned exact permutations for 4 seed keys × 6 sizes (0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8), computed once and
  asserted identical — run under both the 3.10 and 3.14 venv, so the same assertions are the
  cross-interpreter reproduction check.
- Identity for `n <= 1` (`()`/`(0,)`), for several seed keys.
- Every result is a permutation of `range(n)` (sizes up to 64), for several seed keys.
- Deterministic across repeated calls.
- Distinctness across 50 independent keys (no collision) and across the pinned 8-item keys.
- Argument validation (`TypeError` on a non-`str` `seed_key`; `ValueError` on a negative, bool,
  or non-`int` `n`).
- `stable_shuffle`: reorders by the same permutation, doesn't mutate or alias its input, handles
  empty/singleton/tuple input.
- Both names are exported from `jev_cookbook.fixtures.__all__` and identical to the module's.

## Recipe checklist

Not applicable — foundation work (`src/jev_cookbook/`, `tests/`, `docs/fixtures.md`,
`docs/backends.md` only; no recipe touched). Recipe 12's `shuffled_candidates` and recipe 23's
`assign_first_shown` are read-only references for this issue — I read both but changed neither;
they migrate onto this helper in #163, as the issue specifies.

## How it was verified

In a `uv`-managed Python 3.14 venv (`.[dev,ml]` pinned to
`.github/constraints-notebooks.txt`) and a Python 3.10 venv (`.[dev]`), both from this branch's
tip:

- `ruff check .` — all checks passed (both venvs; ruff pinned, same on both).
- `ruff format --check .` — "212 files already formatted" (both venvs); explicitly re-ran on
  `docs/fixtures.md` and `docs/backends.md` alone, since `ruff format` also formats the Python
  fences inside Markdown — "2 files already formatted".
- `python tools/render_catalog.py --check` — clean (no output; this PR touches no recipe or
  README content).
- `python tools/check_hygiene.py <every changed file>` — "Hygiene check passed: 5 file(s)
  scanned."
- `pytest tests/test_permutation.py tests/test_fixtures.py tests/test_backends.py
  tests/test_hygiene.py tests/test_import.py` — 571 passed, on both the 3.10 and the 3.14 venv.
- Full suite, once each, under the shared heavy-job slot: `pytest` — **2169 passed, 3 skipped**
  on 3.14 (87.89s), and the identical **2169 passed, 3 skipped** on 3.10 (97.18s). No leftover
  `pytest`/`execute_notebook` processes after either run.

## Decisions

- **Construction chosen:** hand-rolled Fisher-Yates over `random.Random(seed).random()`, seed =
  first 64 bits of `sha256(seed_key)` as an int — not `random.Random(...).shuffle()`, and not an
  explicit hash-ranked sort. This matches `ScriptedBackend.rng_for`'s and recipe 12's existing
  seeding convention exactly, so there is exactly one derivation of "hash a key into a
  `random.Random` seed" in the codebase for a later reader to learn, not two.
- **Where it lives:** `src/jev_cookbook/fixtures/permutation.py`, re-exported from
  `jev_cookbook.fixtures` (not the top-level `jev_cookbook` package) — it's fixture-authoring
  guidance, same as `load_inputs`/`responses_path`/etc., which the docs already import via
  `from jev_cookbook.fixtures import ...`.
- **`stable_shuffle` return type:** a `tuple`, like `stable_permutation` and like
  `Example.replay_keys` elsewhere in this package — never mutates or aliases its input sequence.
- **No change to `ScriptedBackend.rng_for` or any recipe.** The issue's item 4 is conditional
  ("if any committed replay key depends on `random.shuffle` output..."); the review found none,
  so behaviour is unchanged and only documentation was added, per the issue's own instruction
  not to change behaviour there.
- **Recipe 12/23 migration is explicitly out of scope** (#163), as the issue says; I only read
  both files, never edited them.

## Unfinished / open questions

Nothing is unfinished. One thing worth a second pair of eyes: the "Wave 2" issue comment says
the duplicated helper in recipes 12 and 23 is "written identically" — in fact recipe 12's
`shuffled_candidates` (seeded `rng.shuffle`) and recipe 23's `assign_first_shown` (a per-id hash
bit, deliberately *not* a sequential stream) are different mechanisms, not identical code; only
their seeding *convention* (hash the key, feed a `random.Random`) is shared. I did not change
either file, so this doesn't affect this PR, but the #163 migration will want to confirm which
one `stable_permutation`/`stable_shuffle` should model — this PR's `stable_permutation` behaves
like a generalization of recipe 12's approach (via `random()`, not `shuffle()`), and
`stable_permutation(seed_key, 2)` is a drop-in replacement for recipe 23's binary
`assign_first_shown` had it needed one.

title: Foundation: single-option Choice convention and cross-split replay-key leak check
body:
Closes #175

## What this adds

Two foundation decisions from the recipe 14 review (#173, comment 6075771134), tracked from #80:

1. **Single-option `Choice` convention: rejected.** A `Choice` with fewer than two options now raises `ValueError` at construction ("a Choice needs at least two options; a forced answer belongs to Python, not a request"); `jev_cookbook.answers.choice_confidence` raises the same message for `n < 2` instead of returning `1.0`; a stored `ChoiceAnswer` whose offered option list has one entry fails the same way wherever it is loaded, including by `ReplayBackend`.
   - Where: `src/jev_cookbook/questions.py` (`Choice.__post_init__`, new `MIN_CHOICE_OPTIONS`/`SINGLE_OPTION_MESSAGE`), `src/jev_cookbook/answers.py` (`choice_confidence`; `choice_confidence_bound`'s docstring updated to say its `n = 1` case is now unreachable from `ChoiceAnswer`). No change was needed in `src/jev_cookbook/backends.py`: because `ChoiceAnswer.__post_init__` calls `choice_confidence`, a stored single-option answer already fails there, wrapped as `FixtureError` by `ReplayBackend` -- verified directly rather than assumed.
   - Docs: `docs/backends.md`, new "Single-option Choice" paragraph (under "Questions"), citing recipes 14 (`no_candidates`) and 22 (`no_candidate_resolution`) as the pattern; the "Questions" and "Answers" prose and the Choice confidence formula note are updated to match (2-to-255 options; no more "one option gives 1").
   - Tests: `tests/test_backends.py` -- `test_single_option_choice_is_rejected_at_construction`, `test_choice_confidence_raises_for_a_single_option_instead_of_returning_one`, `test_replay_rejects_a_stored_single_option_choice_with_the_same_message`, `test_single_option_rejection_message_is_identical_everywhere`. Three pre-existing tests that incidentally built a single-option Choice as test data (unrelated to what they were testing) were updated to use two options: `test_choice_validation`, `test_scripted_rejects_bad_scripts`, `test_question_values_are_text_object_array_or_none`.
   - **Scope widened beyond the issue's original allowed paths, by coordinator decision recorded on #175:** fixing this convention broke a non-recipe, non-test consumer outside the original allowed paths -- see "Decisions" below.

2. **Fixture validator: cross-split replay-key leak check.** The validator now also compares `replay_keys` directly across `train`/`validation`/`test` (not just `state`/`fields`), for an example whose entire request is one key (the same restriction the existing key-copy check uses, for the same reason: a multi-key example may legitimately share a *later* key on purpose). This catches recipe 14's exact review finding: `v17` (validation) and `t15` (test) had different `fields` but a byte-identical request, invisible to the content-based rule.
   - Where: `src/jev_cookbook/fixtures/__init__.py` (`_check_examples`).
   - Docs: `docs/fixtures.md`, new "Replay-key leak rule" paragraph beside the existing leak rule.
   - Tests: `tests/test_fixtures.py` -- `test_distinct_replay_keys_across_splits_are_not_a_leak`, `test_a_shared_replay_key_across_splits_is_a_leak`, `test_a_shared_replay_key_in_any_two_of_train_validation_test_is_a_leak` (parametrized train/validation/test pairs), `test_demo_may_share_a_replay_key_with_a_scored_split`, `test_a_shared_replay_key_in_one_split_is_not_a_leak`, `test_a_legitimately_shared_later_request_across_splits_is_not_a_leak`.
   - Verified `python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate --all` clean on both Pythons for every recipe's committed fixtures (all Wave 2 recipes have unique keys across splits, as expected).

## Decisions

- **No recipe or the template constructs a single-option `Choice`.** Checked by grepping every recipe's `helpers.py` for `Choice(` (one call site each) and by running every recipe's own test suite plus `fixtures validate --all` on both Pythons -- all green before and after. Recipes 14 and 22 already avoid it (`no_candidates`, `no_candidate_resolution`).
- **`docs/simulation.md`'s documented example did construct one, deterministically, on its very first step.** `ToyGrid._legal_actions()` returns only `["right"]` at the agent's starting position (`position == 0`), and the example's `run()` loop built a `Choice` from `legal_actions()` on every step without exception. This is shared infrastructure outside the issue's original allowed paths (no recipe imports `ToyGrid`; it is exercised only by `tests/test_simulation.py::test_docs_example_runs_end_to_end`). I stopped and reported this rather than widening scope on my own judgment; the coordinator then explicitly widened the allowed paths for this PR to `src/jev_cookbook/questions.py` (already needed for the constructor check), `docs/simulation.md`, and conditionally `src/jev_cookbook/simulation.py`. The fix was possible in the doc example alone, so `src/jev_cookbook/simulation.py` was not touched: `run()` now takes a step with exactly one legal move directly in Python (`actions.record(move, step=sim.steps, rule="only legal move")`, no `Choice` built, no call spent), matching the recipes 14/22 convention this issue establishes; the surrounding prose explains it and points at `docs/backends.md`. `tests/test_simulation.py::test_docs_example_runs_end_to_end` is updated for the new invariant (a free Python move no longer spends a budget call) and now asserts the short-circuit is actually exercised by the example's own fixed seeds.
- `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py` and `docs/evaluation.md` were not touched (off limits: #161 is editing them concurrently).
- Every other existing public signature is unchanged.

## How it was verified

Base: `main` at `65978eeafb2ed7a8a19d5f02c6ce8087b0f5e943`. Linux, `uv` venvs: `.venv` (Python 3.14, `.[dev,ml]` with `-c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`) and `.venv310` (Python 3.10, `.[dev]`). No `.env`, no key, `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE` unset, default service tier.

```
ruff check .                                   -> All checks passed! (3.14 and 3.10 venvs)
ruff format --check .                          -> N files already formatted (3.14 and 3.10 venvs)
python tools/check_hygiene.py                  -> Hygiene check passed: 304 file(s) scanned. (3.14 and 3.10)
python tools/render_catalog.py --check         -> exit 0 (no output; nothing outside recipes/catalog changed)
pytest tests/test_backends.py tests/test_fixtures.py tests/test_simulation.py
                                                -> 317 passed (3.14), 317 passed (3.10)
pytest recipes/                                -> 643 passed (3.14), 643 passed (3.10)
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate --all -> fixtures valid (mode replay) for all 23 recipes + _template (3.14 and 3.10)
python -m pytest -q (full suite, under the HEAVY slot, nice -n 10 timeout 1500)
                                                -> 2134 passed, 3 skipped in 87.59s (3.14)
```

Nothing was skipped, disabled, or loosened to get a check to pass.

## Recipe checklist

Not applicable: this is foundation work, not a recipe pull request.

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/NN-slug/`... -- N/A (foundation)
- [x] README regenerated... -- N/A (foundation; `README.md` untouched, `render_catalog.py --check` passes)

title: Recipe 22: fabricate vendor, product and version names (R22)
body:
## Finding

Wave 2 consistency review finding **R22** (issue #76, [comment 6079429778](https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/issues/76#issuecomment-6079429778), routed to #163): the merged recipe `recipes/22-cmdb-asset-matching/` used real vendors, real products, and real published build numbers in `build_fixtures.py`'s `ROWS`, `helpers.py`'s `CMDB_RECORDS` and `_PHRASE_ALIASES` tables, and the fixtures themselves — against CONTRIBUTING.md section 5 ("Fabricated names and numbers only"). Examples the review quoted: `Adobe Systems Incorporated | Acrobat | 11.0.23`, `Oracle Corp | Database | 19.3.0.0.0 (19c)`, `SAP SE | ECC | 6.0 EHP8`, `Red Hat, Inc. | RHEL | 8.6`, `Atlassian | Jira Software | 9.4.1`, `MS Corp | SQL Server | SQL2019 CU18 (15.0.4261.1)`, plus Salesforce, Zoom, AgileBits/1Password, Docker, GitHub, GitLab, Notion and Figma, and real legal-name alias entries such as `"adobe systems incorporated"`, `"red hat, inc."`, `"sap ag"`, `"microsoft corporation"`, `"erp central component"`.

Refs #163. Refs #22.

## Why this is a foundation pull request, not a recipe pull request

Issue #163's own body frames every item in its sweep as "one foundation pull request per the allowlist (foundation PRs are not subject to it) or several small recipe PRs" — recipe 22 is already published (PR #178, merged), so this is a fix to an existing folder, not a new recipe.

I checked `tools/check_recipe_scope.py` / `docs/notebook-ci.md` directly rather than assume: the scope check classifies a pull request as a **recipe pull request** only when *both* markers hold — branch `recipe/<slug>` **and** a GitHub closing keyword (`Closes`/`Fixes`/`Resolves`, not `Refs`) for an issue 1–60 — and then requires the branch to equal `recipe/` plus the exact catalog slug (`recipe/22-cmdb-asset-matching`). That exact branch name already exists on `origin` from the original, merged PR #178 at a commit (`de82927`) that is **not** an ancestor of current `main`, so reusing it would need a force-push, which the builder rules forbid. I could not satisfy "branch starts with `recipe/`" and "branch equals `recipe/22-cmdb-asset-matching`" at the same time without force-pushing over someone else's merged history, so per the brief's instruction ("if the check requires `Closes #NN` for an open issue, STOP and report rather than inventing one") I stopped and used the other lane the check itself defines: this PR's branch does **not** start with `recipe/`, and the body uses `Refs`, not `Closes`, for both #163 and #22 — so neither scope marker holds and `tools/check_recipe_scope.py` classifies it as a foundation pull request (verified locally: `scope ok: foundation pull request: the recipe allowlist does not apply`). Allowed path is still self-restricted to `recipes/22-cmdb-asset-matching/**` exactly as the brief specifies, even though the foundation classification doesn't mechanically enforce it.

Issue #22 is already closed (the recipe shipped); this PR does not reopen or re-close it.

## What changed

Every real vendor, product, edition and version/build number was replaced with an invented equivalent, keeping the recipe's structure and every hard case exactly as it was: vendor aliases, version-format variants, edition names, the three-way major-version family, the edition sibling, the lexical look-alike, the zero-candidate assets, and the confidently-wrong `no_match`. Fixture row ids were renamed to match (e.g. `v01-acrobat` → `v01-inkpress`). Authored probabilities were **not** touched, and no replay-key collision or retrieval-ordering drift ended up forcing any evaluation number to change (see "Numbers" below) — every published number is unchanged; only the underlying fixture replay keys changed, which is expected from renaming the state text.

### Mapping (real → fabricated), for verification

| Adobe | Candlewood |
| Oracle | Thornfield |
| SAP | Ashgrove |

**Decoys (zero-candidate assets, never in the CMDB pool)**

| Notion Labs / Notion | Driftnote Labs / Driftnote |

**Decoys (retrieved as a candidate, but not a match)**

**Legal-suffix and abbreviation aliases (`helpers._PHRASE_ALIASES`)**
| Real | Fabricated |
|---|---|
| `microsoft corporation`, `microsoft corp`, `msft` | `northcastle corporation`, `northcastle corp`, `nstl` |

The real `"red hat"` → `"redhat"` self-collapse entry (needed because the real vendor name is two words, so it and the `"rhel"` expansion must land on the same single token) has no fabricated counterpart: `Redfern` is already one word, so `"rfos"` expands straight to `"redfern enterprise os"`. 18 alias entries instead of the original 19 for that structural reason, noted here so a reviewer doesn't read it as a dropped case.

**Major versions** were also bumped by a few digits each (e.g. SQL Server 2016/2019/2022 → LedgerStack Server 2017/2020/2023; RHEL 8 → Enterprise OS 9) so they don't coincidentally equal the real products' real current versions now that the vendor/product names are fictional.

**Fixture row ids** were renamed to match their new product (full list in the diff); the generic ids (`v13-lookalike-wrong`, `v14/v15/t12/t18-zero-candidate`, `t11-lookalike-correct`, `d01-lookalike`, `d02-zero-candidate`, `d03-decoy-many`) were already free of real names and are unchanged.

### One naming collision caught and fixed before shipping

My first pass named the SAP ECC analogue "Enterprise Resource Nexus" — which accidentally shares the word "Enterprise" with the Red Hat Enterprise Linux analogue ("Enterprise OS"), a collision the real names never had (`ERP Central Component` has no word in common with `Enterprise Linux`). That inflated several assets' retrieved-candidate counts (`candidate count distribution` changed from `{0:5, 2:21, 3:15, 5:2}` to `{0:5, 2:19, 3:9, 4:6, 5:4}`) and shifted the gate-sweep's intermediate cut-off points, even though the final chosen gate and every reported evaluation number were unaffected. Renamed to "Processwell Core" / `PWCR` (no shared words with anything else in the fabricated catalog), re-ran, and the candidate-count distribution, gold-position table, both baselines, and every evaluation number came back byte-for-byte identical to the pre-fix numbers (see below).

## Numbers (unchanged, verified identical before/after)

- Candidate-count distribution, all 43 fixtures: `{0: 5, 2: 21, 3: 15, 5: 2}` (`MAX_CANDIDATES` reached by `t13-forge-decoy`, `d03-decoy-many`)
- Gold-match position, 40 scored assets: `no_match: 10, position 1: 24, position 2: 4, position 3: 2`
- Chosen confidence gate: `0.7450` (over 16 real-candidate validation matches, 1 wrong)
- Validation: link accuracy `0.9500`; baselines `0.7000` / `0.8000`; coverage `0.9000`, accuracy `1.0000`, risk `0.0000`, false-link rate `0.0000`
- Test: link accuracy `0.8500`; baselines `0.7000` / `0.7500`; coverage `0.8500`, accuracy `0.8824`, risk `0.1176`, false-link rate `0.0833`

title: Recipe 19: CI failure classification
body:
Closes #19

## What this adds

`recipes/19-ci-failure-classification/`: a Level 2 `Choice` recipe that classifies a
continuous-integration failure, from a trimmed excerpt of its log, as `test_regression`,
`dependency_problem`, `infrastructure_failure`, or `unknown`, and picks the next diagnostic
workflow from a fixed table keyed by outcome.

- Python trims each build's log down to the excerpt it actually sends to Jev *before* it builds
  the request (`helpers.trim_log`); the untrimmed log is kept in `fixtures/inputs.jsonl`
  (`fields.full_log`) so the trimming is checked against real data, not merely illustrated.
  `trim_log` keeps a window around every line naming a dependency or infrastructure problem,
  wherever it falls, plus a window around the first line naming a test failure — a fixture
  (`v-dep-04-fartrim`, and a parallel one on `test`) is built so the decisive line sits more
  than twenty lines past the first failure, to make the point that a "window around the first
  failure only" trim would miss it.
- `helpers.classify` logs the table's workflow to a simulated `jev_cookbook.simulation.ActionLog`
  only when the answer names a workflow Python recognises *and* is confident enough; otherwise
  it goes to a `ReviewQueue` with the reason recorded. `unknown` is the one exception: it is
  always delivered, workflow logged, never reviewed, because its workflow (`manual_triage`)
  commits to no automated remedy, so there is nothing a confidence gate would be protecting
  (CONTRIBUTING.md section 4). Because that is a review-branch *other than* the confidence gate,
  selective coverage/accuracy/risk are reported with `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes`
  from `classify`'s own accept/review split, not `evaluate_selective`; the notebook also computes
  `evaluate_selective` on the same `test` split and prints both, so the claim that they can
  disagree is shown as numbers (1 of 19 answered vs. 6 of 19), not only argued.
- Hard cases from the issue's build notes, all in `fixtures/`: a dependency error that surfaces
  as a failing test (gold `dependency_problem`, with a stored answer confidently and wrongly
  calling it `test_regression` on both `validation` and `test`); an infrastructure failure that
  looks like a test failure (runner lost mid-test); flaky/ambiguous logs with gold `unknown`;
  and the far-decisive-line trimming case above. `test` also carries a build whose gold label is
  `test_regression` but whose stored answer confidently calls it `unknown` — accepted by
  `classify` regardless of the threshold, since `unknown` is never gated, which is a different,
  structural kind of miss from the gated one.
- A trivial majority-class baseline and a keyword-regex baseline (reusing `trim_log`'s own
  patterns, now public: `helpers.DEPENDENCY_RE`/`INFRASTRUCTURE_RE`/`FAILURE_RE`) are computed
  and printed against the raw choice's accuracy on `test`, with an honest account of where the
  one-build margin over the keyword baseline comes from (three flaky builds it misreads as
  `test_regression`, against two hard cases it happens to get right where the stored answers do
  not).

## Fixtures

40 examples: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo` (shown but never scored). Every `validation`
and `test` example has a gold label; both wrong-and-confident hard cases (one per kind of miss)
sit on `test`, giving non-zero selective risk there; gold is not concentrated on one outcome
(roughly 5/5/5/4 per split).

## Evaluation numbers (all derived in the notebook, not typed)

- Threshold (chosen on `validation`, `select_confidence_threshold(..., target_accuracy=1.0)`,
  frozen before `test` is touched): **0.8400**.
- `validation` (selection step; not a reported result): raw accuracy 0.8947; `unknown` (final,
  no gate) 4 of 19; `review` 14 of 19; `evaluate_outcomes`: answered 5 of 19 (coverage 0.2632),
  accuracy 1.0000, risk 0.0000.
- `test` (reported; threshold frozen): raw accuracy 0.8947; `unknown` 5 of 19; `review` 13 of 19;
  `evaluate_outcomes`: answered 6 of 19 (coverage 0.3158), accuracy 0.8333, **risk 0.1667**.
  `evaluate_selective` on the same split/threshold: answered 1 of 19 (coverage 0.0526), accuracy
  1.0000, risk 0.0000 — shown side by side in the notebook as the concrete divergence.
- Confusion matrix on `test` (gold rows × predicted columns, order `test_regression`,
  `dependency_problem`, `infrastructure_failure`, `unknown`):
  `[[4,0,0,1],[1,4,0,0],[0,0,5,0],[0,0,0,4]]`. Per-class precision/recall/f1/support:
  `test_regression` 0.800/0.800/0.800/5; `dependency_problem` 1.000/0.800/0.889/5;
  `infrastructure_failure` 1.000/1.000/1.000/5; `unknown` 0.800/1.000/0.889/4.
- Baselines on `test`: majority-class (`test_regression` for every build) 0.2632; keyword-regex
  (no excerpt, `trim_log`'s own patterns) 0.8421; raw choice 0.8947 — beats both.
- Request count: exactly **40** in live mode (one per fixture; each example decided once and
  reused). That is **above** the live backend's default budget of 25; the README tells the
  reader to raise `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` to at least 40 first.

## Decisions a later builder should know about

- `unknown` is delivered as a **final** result, never reviewed, whatever its confidence
  (CONTRIBUTING.md section 4: its workflow, `manual_triage`, commits to no automated remedy, so
  there is nothing for a gate to protect). The other three outcomes are gated on confidence
  before Python logs that it would act. This is the review-branch-other-than-the-gate case, so
  selective metrics use `evaluate_outcomes`, not `evaluate_selective` — both are computed and
  printed on `test` so the divergence is a number, not a claim.
- `helpers.DEPENDENCY_RE`, `INFRASTRUCTURE_RE`, `FAILURE_RE` are public (no leading underscore)
  because the notebook's keyword-regex baseline reuses them directly, rather than re-deriving a
  second, possibly-drifting set of patterns.
- The Choice `instructions` text deliberately does not claim the excerpt is "trimmed to the
  lines that matter": for the inconclusive/flaky fixtures `trim_log` falls back to the first few
  lines of the log, with no decisive content found, so that phrase would not have been literally
  true of every state.
- `tests/test_helpers.py` pins every reason string (`"confident match"`, `"confidence below the
  threshold"`, `"no option fits"`, `"not a workflow Python may use"`) with `==`, one test each,
  and a parametrized test over the three gated outcomes plus a boundary test at the threshold.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/19-ci-failure-classification/` (checked locally with
  `tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD`: `scope ok`), plus the generated
  README regions the integration worker will add
- [ ] README regenerated with `tools/render_catalog.py` — not run by this builder; `Catalog
  (README is current)` is expected red until the integration worker updates this branch
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/19-ci-failure-classification/`
  paths, every mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, no key, no network (`tools/execute_notebook.py`, run
  twice, byte-identical)
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions (`get_backend`/`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE`)
- [x] Every response fixture's provenance is `synthetic`; `run_header` states the mode
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost anywhere in this folder
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the named hard cases, carry gold labels
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (`ActionLog`, `ReviewQueue`, both
      `executed: False`/never-deleted by construction)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, plus the majority-class and keyword-regex baselines
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on #19 is met (see below)

## Acceptance criteria (issue #19)

- [x] `notebook.ipynb` runs top to bottom offline, no key/network, outputs committed — executed
  twice with `tools/execute_notebook.py`, byte-identical
- [x] Live mode opt-in, same question definitions — `get_backend`/`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE` unchanged
  from the offline path; README states the exact request count (40) and the budget note
- [x] Fixtures synthetic, hard cases named in the build notes present, gold labels, pass the
  validator — `python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/19-ci-failure-classification`:
  `fixtures valid (mode replay)`
- [x] Every response fixture records provenance (`synthetic`); notebook states its mode via
  `run_header`
- [x] Evaluation: accuracy and a confusion matrix — printed as a table beside the plotted figure
- [x] Candidate sets (the four outcomes) assembled by Python, shown to the reader
- [x] `unknown`/review exercised by several fixtures, reported separately — 4–5 `unknown` and
  13–14 `review` per split, printed as their own counts, not folded into coverage/accuracy
- [x] No Jev quality/latency/cost claim without recorded live inference; synthetic metrics
  labelled as pipeline checks (`check`, `selection`, both on validation lines)
- [x] README says what it teaches, how to run it, what was/was not measured live
- [x] PR changes only `recipes/19-ci-failure-classification/`

## How it was verified

All commands run from the repository root in `recipes/19-ci-failure-classification`'s own clean
venvs (`uv venv --python 3.14 .venv`, `.[dev,ml]` under
`.github/constraints-notebooks.txt`; `uv venv --python 3.10 .venv310`, `.[dev]`):

```
python recipes/19-ci-failure-classification/build_fixtures.py      # 40 examples, 38 labels, 40 responses
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/19-ci-failure-classification
                                                                     # fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/19-ci-failure-classification -q                     # 23 passed (3.14 and 3.10)
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/19-ci-failure-classification
                                                                     # run twice, byte-identical
ruff check .                                                        # All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                                               # (all files) already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py                                      # Hygiene check passed
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/19-ci-failure-classification --body-file <file>
                                                                     # scope ok
pytest -q   (full suite, under the shared heavy slot)               # 1771 passed, 3 skipped
```

`build_fixtures.py` also reproduced byte-identical `fixtures/` under the 3.10 venv.

Expect `Catalog (README is current)` red until the integration worker regenerates `README.md`;

title: Recipe 23: Pairwise answer evaluation
body:
Closes #23

## What this adds

`recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation/`: a Level 2 `Choice` recipe that compares two candidate
answers to a question against one explicit rubric criterion, with outcomes `a`, `b`, `tie`, and
`insufficient_evidence`.

**The question.** Jev is asked a purely positional `Choice` over `{first, second, tie,
insufficient_evidence}`: given the stated criterion, does the first candidate answer shown
satisfy it better, the second, are they equal, or is neither sufficient to judge. It never sees
which candidate is "a" and which is "b" — that identity, and which one is shown first, is
Python-owned bookkeeping (`fields["a_shown_first"]`) that never reaches the model. Every
comparison makes **two** requests: the candidates in one order, then the same two with the order
swapped (`helpers.build_state(fields, swap=True)`), so every example lists two replay keys, in
request order, per `docs/fixtures.md`.

**The rule (`helpers.judge_pair`).** Checked in order: (1) do the two requests agree with each
other once relabelled back to `a`/`b`/`tie`/`insufficient_evidence` — if not, `review` with the
reason `"orders disagree"`, whatever either confidence is; (2) among agreeing pairs,
`insufficient_evidence` is accepted immediately, with no confidence check — choosing it promotes
neither candidate and has no side effect, so there is nothing left for a gate to protect
(CONTRIBUTING.md section 4); (3) every other agreed label (`a`, `b`, `tie`) needs the lower of the
two requests' confidences to clear a threshold chosen on `validation`, below which it is `review`
with the reason `"confidence below the threshold"`.

**Fixtures.** 40 comparisons (19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`), 80 stored responses (two per
comparison). Gold labels: `a` 10, `b` 10, `tie` 9, `insufficient_evidence` 9 — balanced, not
always one option. `helpers.assign_first_shown` decides which candidate is shown first from
nothing but each comparison's id and position (never the gold label or candidate text); the
notebook prints the resulting gold-label × first-position table, and the share of "a shown
first" is 0.500 / 0.500 / 0.556 / 0.444 across the four gold labels — no visible correlation.
Hard cases: several comparisons where the two orders disagree (position bias, authored by hand
to exercise the swap check — the notebook says plainly this is not a finding about Jev), one
comparison (`t04`) where both orders agree, confidently, on the wrong candidate (the fixture
responsible for this recipe's non-zero risk on `test`), and a matching but lower-confidence
wrong-and-consistent comparison (`v04`) on `validation` that sets the threshold in the first
place. `build_fixtures.py` keeps inputs/labels generation separate from responses generation,
following the template, and is byte-identical when run under Python 3.10 and 3.14 (verified; see
below).

**Evaluation**, per the issue's acceptance criteria:

- Accuracy and Cohen's kappa (`jev_cookbook.evaluation.cohens_kappa`), on two populations: *all
  first-order verdicts* (every comparison's first, unswapped request, whether or not it agrees
  with its own swapped-order twin) and *accepted verdicts* (what `judge_pair` actually reports).
  Validation: first-order accuracy 0.8421 / kappa 0.7889; accepted 1.0000 / 1.0000 (14 of 19).
  Test: first-order 0.7368 / kappa 0.6481; accepted 0.9231 / kappa 0.8968 (13 of 19) — the swap
  check visibly earns its keep on both splits.
- Order-consistency rate (consistent pairs / all pairs): validation 0.7895 (15/19), test 0.7368
  (14/19) — deliberately different between splits.
- Coverage/accuracy/risk from the rule's own outcomes, `evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)`,
  because `judge_pair`'s review branch is more than a confidence gate. Validation: coverage
  0.7368, accuracy 1.0000, risk 0.0000 (by construction of the threshold). Test: coverage 0.6842,
  **accuracy 0.9231, risk 0.0769** (non-zero, from `t04`).
- `evaluate_selective`'s gate-only view is computed and shown beside `evaluate_outcomes` because
  the two numbers differ (checked, not assumed): the gate-only view wrongly *accepts* 5 test
  comparisons whose orders disagree but whose confidence clears the gate, and wrongly *rejects*
  1 (`t15`) whose orders agree on `insufficient_evidence` at a confidence below the gate — two
  different divergence mechanisms, both printed and explained.
- Two trivial baselines on `test` ("always pick `a`": 0.2632; "the longer answer wins": 0.3684),
  both clearly beaten by the accepted-verdicts accuracy (0.9231).
- Review outcomes reported separately by reason, on both splits.
- The threshold-selection cell reuses the frozen gate to classify the two demo comparisons shown
  earlier (one accepted, one sent to review for disagreement), and "Next steps" names a looser
  `target_accuracy` (0.9) that is verified to actually move the gate (0.5300 → 0.5200).

**Live budget.** Every comparison needs two requests; this notebook makes exactly 80 in live mode
(two for each of the 40 comparisons, including the two `demo` ones), counted by a request
counter in the setup cell and printed in "What was and was not measured" (`Requests made in this
run: 80`). The README tells the reader to set `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=80` or higher.

## Decisions a later builder should know about

- **`insufficient_evidence` is final without a confidence gate, by choice.** The issue leaves this
  open ("your call, defended"). I treated it the same way the template's `none` option and
  recipe 08's `no_match` are allowed to be treated under CONTRIBUTING.md section 4: it has no
  side effect (nothing is promoted), so there is nothing a confidence gate would protect. It is
  still scored against the gold label like any other accepted verdict (correct only when the gold
  label is also `insufficient_evidence`) — "not scored" in the issue's phrasing refers to the
  absence of a side effect, not to exemption from the accuracy/kappa numbers.
- **Positional options, not `a`/`b` options.** Jev's `Choice` options are `first`/`second`/`tie`/
  `insufficient_evidence`, not `a`/`b`/`tie`/`insufficient_evidence`: Jev has no way to know which
  candidate is "a", so asking it to name `a` or `b` directly would be meaningless. Python
  relabels after each request using which candidate was actually first in *that* request
  (`helpers.relabel`, `helpers.first_is_a`).
- **The two requests are not a "dependent follow-up."** TypeSafe's primitives page (S02) reserves
  that term for a request Python cannot build until it has an earlier answer; here the swap is
  decided in advance. They still need two separate requests because they describe two different
  states (the candidates' positions differ), not because of any dependency — the notebook says
  this explicitly to avoid overclaiming S02 doesn't cover this case.
- **Seed choice.** `helpers.ORDER_SEED = 40` was chosen (by a small search over seeds, done while
  authoring fixtures, not at runtime) because it gives a well-balanced gold-label × first-position
  table on this specific, small (38-example) fixture set; the assignment function itself never
  looks at the gold label or candidate text, only at ids and their order.

## How it was verified

All commands run from the repository root, inside the recipe's own venvs (`uv venv --python 3.14
.venv`, `uv venv --python 3.10 .venv310`), under the shared `HEAVY.lock` for the notebook
executions and the full suite.

- `python recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation/build_fixtures.py` — byte-identical output on
  Python 3.10 and 3.14 (compared by SHA-256 of all three fixture files).
- `python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation` — `fixtures
  valid (mode replay)`.
- `pytest recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation` — 40 passed, on both 3.10 and 3.14.
- `python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation`, run twice — exit 0
  both times, byte-identical (`diff` empty), both before and after `ruff format`.
- `ruff check .` — all checks passed. `ruff format --check .` — all files already formatted.
- `python tools/check_hygiene.py` — passed, 196 files scanned.
- `python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD --branch
  recipe/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation --body-file <this body>` — `scope ok: recipe pull request
  for #23 (23-pairwise-answer-evaluation): 9 changed paths`.
- Full `pytest` (whole repository) — 1751 passed, 3 skipped (pre-existing, unrelated to this recipe), on both Python 3.14 and Python 3.10, in 85.58s and 97.58s respectively.
- `grep -rn TODO recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation` — empty.
- Did **not** run `tools/render_catalog.py`; `Catalog (README is current)` is expected red until
  the integration worker runs, per CONTRIBUTING.md's generated-README exception.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation/` (verified by the scope
      check and by `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD`); the generated README regions are for
      the integration worker, not this pull request
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` — not run by this pull request
      (generated-README exception); expected red until the integration worker runs
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation/`
      paths, every mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change, no rename or deletion out of scope
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network (verified twice,
      byte-identical)
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions (`get_backend` swap only)
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states its mode
      via `run_header`
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference (none made;
      this recipe has no recorded fixtures)
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases (position-bias disagreement, a confident
      wrong-and-consistent pair, several `insufficient_evidence` pairs), and carry gold labels
      for every scored comparison
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (no side effect exists in this
      recipe — it only reports a verdict)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, with two trivial baselines (always-`a`, longer-answer-wins)
      clearly beaten by the accepted-verdicts accuracy
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see the issue checklist mapping below)

### Issue #23 acceptance criteria

- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, no key, no network, outputs committed

title: Recipe 22: CMDB asset matching
body:
Closes #22

## What this adds

`recipes/22-cmdb-asset-matching/`: a Level 2 `Choice` recipe that links an observed software asset description (vendor, product, version, edition, exactly as a discovery scan would report them) to a canonical CMDB record from a per-asset candidate list, or reports `no_match`.

- **Retrieval (`helpers.shortlist`)**: normalized vendor/product token overlap (lowercasing, folding vendor aliases such as `"MSFT"`/`"Red Hat, Inc."`/`"SAP SE"` and corporate suffixes), ranked, tie-broken by record id, capped at `MAX_CANDIDATES = 5`. The candidate count is **not fixed**: it is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 across this recipe's own fixtures (never padded with zero-overlap records to hit a target size).
- **Single-option `Choice` is never sent (issue #175's preferred convention)**: when `shortlist` returns no candidate at all, `helpers.no_candidate_resolution` resolves the asset directly to `no_match` and no request is ever made (4 of the 38 scored fixtures, plus 1 of the 2 demo fixtures, take this path; `build_questions` raises if ever called with an empty candidate list).
- **The version family**: CMDB-01/02/03 are the same vendor and product (Microsoft SQL Server), differing only by major version (2016/2019/2022). Retrieval never looks at version, so the three always tie and always appear together, tie-broken by id — which is also why the gold match for this family lands at shortlist position 2 or 3 in several fixtures, not always 1 (printed, derived-in-code distribution table in the notebook: position 1 ×24, position 2 ×2, position 3 ×2, not-applicable/no_match ×10, over the 38 scored assets).
- **Rule (`helpers.match_record`)**: links a confident real candidate (the one outcome with a simulated side effect — an `ActionLog` entry, never executed); reports `no_match` as a final, un-gated result whatever its confidence, because the only effect of choosing it is a non-mutating `ReviewQueue` "backlog" entry (no write to the CMDB) — the CONTRIBUTING.md §4 fallback clause; sends a confident answer naming something outside the retrieved candidates to `review` (defensive membership check, unreachable through replay/live but tested directly); sends a real candidate below the confidence gate to `review` with reason exactly `"confidence below the threshold"`. `evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)` is used (not `evaluate_selective`) because the rule's review branch is more than a single confidence gate.
- **Two trivial, Jev-free baselines** (`baseline_always_top`, `baseline_overlap_cutoff`) are computed and printed in the notebook alongside the rule's own **link accuracy** (raw choice vs. gold, before the gate), on both splits. Neither baseline reads version or edition, so neither can ever tell CMDB-01/02/03 apart; the rule's stored answers, which do read version text, clearly beat both:
  - validation: baseline (always-top) 0.7368, baseline (overlap cutoff 0.6) 0.8421, rule 0.9474
  - test: baseline (always-top) 0.7368, baseline (overlap cutoff 0.6) 0.7895, rule 0.8421
- **Evaluation**: link accuracy, the false-link rate (`helpers.false_link_rate` — an accepted link to the wrong record; reporting `no_match` for a real match is not a false link), `no_match` reported separately (precision/recall/support), and selective coverage/accuracy/risk from `evaluate_outcomes`. Gate chosen on `validation` (`select_confidence_threshold(target_accuracy=1.0)` over real-candidate answers only) is non-vacuous there (2 of 19 reviewed) and `test` risk is non-zero (0.125) with a real false link (0.0909 false-link rate) the gate does not catch.

## Fixture design (40 total: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`)

Fixed CMDB pool of 15 canonical records (10 "focal" + 5 same-vendor siblings, so that retrieving a record's own asset also retrieves a real second candidate to discriminate against, rather than standing alone against `no_match`). Hard cases named in the issue and in the build notes:

- Two (here, three) records differing only by major version — exercised above.
- A fixture where the observed version is missing (`"not reported"`): this recipe's **policy** is that Python never asks Jev to guess a major version it cannot see, so the gold label is `no_match`; one such fixture (`v12`) is answered correctly, and one (`t10`, required) is answered **confidently wrong** — a real false link, since no version was reported to justify it.
- A lexical look-alike: "Acrobat Reader" is a different, free product from the paid "Acrobat" the catalog holds, but shares enough wording to be retrieved as a candidate (`v13`, the validation set's deliberate wrong answer that calibrates the gate; `t11`, the same trap read correctly).
- Assets whose true record is outside the whole candidate universe (gold `no_match`, zero or several weak decoy candidates): `v14`/`v15`/`t12`/`t18` (zero candidates, no request at all), `v16`/`t13` (Microsoft Teams / GitHub Enterprise Server, each retrieving 3–4 real decoys by shared generic words).
- A confidently-wrong false link, a wrong-and-caught low-confidence answer, and a wrong, confident `no_match` on a real match (bypasses the gate entirely, the same shape as recipe 18's `t11-dup-auth-missed`) — all in `test`, each a different failure mode.
- `replay_keys` never repeat across `validation`/`test` (checked by a dedicated test, since the fixture validator's own leak rule does not yet compare keys directly — issue #175 point 2).

## Decisions

- `OVERLAP_CUTOFF = 0.6` for `baseline_overlap_cutoff`: every genuine self-named match in this recipe's fixtures scores a clean 1.0 (vendor aliasing and version/edition wording are the only sources of textual noise; product names are never abbreviated in a way that would dilute token overlap), while every decoy/look-alike scores at most 0.5 — 0.6 sits cleanly between the two.
- `MAX_CANDIDATES = 5`; the catalog's own structure (3-way version family, 2-record sibling pairs) means the fixtures exercise 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 candidates, not 5 — noted honestly in the notebook rather than forced.
- The "unmatched asset" backlog is a second `jev_cookbook.simulation.ReviewQueue` instance (distinct from the uncertain-answer review queue), reused for a different purpose on the strength that neither queue performs or represents a write to the CMDB — only the `ActionLog` entry for a `linked` outcome does that (simulated, never executed).
- No confusion matrix: with 15 real-record labels plus `no_match`, a full matrix was judged less readable than the baseline comparison and the `no_match`-specific precision/recall the issue asks for; happy to add one if review wants it.

python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/22-cmdb-asset-matching   # fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/22-cmdb-asset-matching                         # 45 passed (3.14 and 3.10)

ruff format --check .                                        # all files already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py                                # Hygiene check passed: 223 files

  --branch recipe/22-cmdb-asset-matching --body-file <this file>   # scope ok: 9 changed paths

title: Recipe 21: Quiz answer adjudication
body:
Closes #21

## What this adds

`recipes/21-quiz-answer-adjudication/`: a `Choice` recipe that adjudicates a typed quiz response
against a Python-assembled candidate set of accepted phrasings. Python checks a normalised exact
match first (case, whitespace, punctuation, a leading article folded away); only a response the
normaliser cannot settle is sent to Jev, which picks one of four fixed outcomes: `match`,
`partial_match`, `no_match`, `needs_review`. A question whose accepted answer is a number is
never sent to Jev at all, settled or not (S07: "Jev is not a calculator"), so every one of those
is graded by Python's own number parser.

## Decisions

- **`needs_review` is never a final grade.** CONTRIBUTING.md section 4 treats awarding or
  withholding a point as a side effect, so both of this rule's review conditions (Jev choosing
  `needs_review` outright, or a confidence below the gate for any of the other three choices)
  send a response to a simulated `ReviewQueue`, never to a reported grade.
- **Hedge policy.** A response that hedges between two options is always graded `needs_review` in
  this recipe's fixtures, never `no_match`, applied consistently across every hedge fixture:
  naming the right answer alongside a wrong one is not the same claim as being simply wrong.
- **`evaluate_outcomes`, not `evaluate_selective`, for the reported selective metrics.** The rule
  has an unconditional review branch beyond the confidence gate (Jev choosing `needs_review`
  outright), so `evaluate_selective` would silently disagree with what the rule actually does.
  The notebook does not just argue this: it computes both on the same responses and prints them
  side by side. They coincide on `validation` (no called response there has Jev confidently
  choosing `needs_review` above the gate) and disagree on `test` because of `t12-reef-hedge`
  (Jev confidently chooses `needs_review`, 0.80, well above the frozen gate; `evaluate_selective`
  would count it answered and right, `evaluate_outcomes` correctly reports it as reviewed, not
  answered).
- **Two trivial baselines, both chosen on `validation`'s called responses and reported on
  `test`'s:** a majority-class baseline (0.2500) and a string-similarity baseline using
  `difflib.SequenceMatcher` (0.6250, its structural ceiling: it can only ever say `match` or
  `no_match`, and 3 of `test`'s 8 called responses are `partial_match`/`needs_review`). This
  recipe's rule, agreement with gold on the same responses: 0.7500, clearly above both.
- **Gold label position.** The correct option sits in all four positions of the fixed option
  order (`match`, `partial_match`, `no_match`, `needs_review`) among the fixtures sent to Jev,
  checked by `tests/test_helpers.py::test_the_gold_label_is_not_concentrated_in_one_option_position`,
  so the fixture set cannot be gamed by a rule (or a model) that always trusts the first option
  (S07's documented option-order bias).
- **Numeric questions never reach Jev.** `helpers.settle` resolves every `NUMBER`-kind question
  (digits or the words zero to twenty) to `match`/`no_match` in Python, always, which is also why
  none of the 6 number-kind fixtures ever appear in the request count.

## Fixture counts and numbers (from the executed notebook)

- 40 fixtures: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`.
- Settled without a model call: 11 of 19 `validation`, 11 of 19 `test` (22 of 38 scored).
- Requests made by the whole notebook: **17** (8 `validation` + 8 `test` + 1 `demo`), well under
  the live default budget of 25.
- Confidence gate, chosen on `validation`: **0.5733**.
- Agreement with the gold label: `validation` 0.9474 (18/19, a selection step), `test` 0.8947
  (17/19).
- Selective metrics among responses sent to Jev (`evaluate_outcomes`): `validation` coverage
  0.6250, accuracy 1.0000, risk 0.0000; `test` coverage 0.7500, accuracy 0.8333, **risk 0.1667**
  (non-zero on purpose: `t04-capital-wrong-confident` is a stored `match` at confidence 0.7467
  where the gold label is `no_match`).
- `evaluate_selective` on the same `test` responses: coverage 0.8750, accuracy 0.8571, risk
  0.1429 — disagreeing with `evaluate_outcomes` exactly as described above.

## Checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/21-quiz-answer-adjudication/` (verified with
  `tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD`: `scope ok`). The generated README
  regions are for the integration worker, not this PR.
- [ ] README regenerated with `tools/render_catalog.py` — not run by this builder; expected next,
  by the integration worker, per the generated-README exception.
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/21-quiz-answer-adjudication/`
  paths, all mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change.
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, no key, no network; executed twice, byte-identical.
- [x] Live path is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`) and uses the same question
  definitions as the offline path (same `helpers.build_questions`).
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states its mode
  in the first cell's `run_header` output.
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost anywhere; every metric is labelled a
  pipeline check in this synthetic run.
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases the issue names (misspellings, alternative
  names, over-specific answers, hedges, wrong entities, numeric responses), and carry gold labels
  for every scored example.
- [x] Python owns every side effect: `helpers.adjudicate` is the only place a grade or a
  `ReviewQueue` submission is decided; nothing real is sent, moved, or changed.
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, plus two trivial baselines (majority-class and

  shown to the reader (the "Jev sees" state dump, and the normaliser demo).

title: Recipe 20: Claim support classification
body:
Closes #20

## What this adds

Recipe 20, "Claim support classification": a `Choice` recipe that classifies whether a provided
passage `supports`, `contradicts`, or leaves `unresolved` a specific claim, carrying the passage's
own identifier (`passage_id`) from input to output unchanged on every outcome (`helpers.Classification`;
`tests/test_helpers.py::test_the_passage_id_is_carried_through_for_every_outcome`). The question is
designed from TypeSafe's citation-checking cookbook pattern (S06,
`https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md`): one `Choice` question (`relation`) over
`claim` and `passage`, with the third option widened from that pattern's "says nothing" to this
use case's own `unresolved`, which also covers a passage that only supports a narrower/weaker
version of the claim and a passage that shares the claim's words while addressing something else.
The notebook and README say so explicitly where the question is defined.

`helpers.py` carries one rule, `classify`, that accepts the chosen relation when its confidence
clears a threshold chosen on `validation` (`select_confidence_threshold`, `target_accuracy=1.0`:
**0.4000**) and frozen before `test`; every option is one Python is willing to report, so the only
review branch is the confidence gate, and `evaluate_selective` is used as-is (no
`evaluate_outcomes` distinction to argue, per the brief guidance).

Fixtures (40 total: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`) include every hard case the issue
names: `v07`/`t07` and `v18`/`t18` (on topic, does not settle the claim → `unresolved`), `v08`/`t08`
(supports only a narrower/weaker version of the claim → `unresolved`) paired with `v09`/`t09`
(supports a *stronger* claim, which does entail the weaker one asked about → `supports`), `v10`/`t10`
(contradicts by a date), `v11`/`t11` (lexical look-alike: shares the claim's keywords but is about a
different population → `unresolved`), and `t16-confident-wrong` (stored `supports` at confidence
0.80 where gold is `contradicts`) so selective risk on `test` is non-zero. `v16-low-confidence-wrong`
makes the validation-side threshold selection non-vacuous: it is the one wrong `validation` answer
the selector has to exclude, and in doing so it also excludes one correct, low-confidence
`validation` example (`v08`) as a side effect.

Gold labels are balanced across the three classes in the fixed `OPTIONS` order (`supports`,
`contradicts`, `unresolved`): 7/5/7 on `validation`, 6/6/7 on `test`. A majority-label baseline
(chosen on `validation`: always guess `supports`, tied with `unresolved` at seven examples each)
is printed and clearly beaten by the rule's raw accuracy (baseline 0.3158 vs. 0.9474 on `test`).

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/20-claim-support-classification/` (nothing else outside the
      recipe folder; the generated README regions are left to the integration worker)

      red (`Catalog (README is current)`) until the integration worker updates this branch

      paths, all mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change (`check_recipe_scope.py` confirms: "scope
      ok: recipe pull request for #20 (20-claim-support-classification): 0 changed paths" outside it)
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which mode
      it ran in
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference (none here;
      every number is labelled a pipeline check)
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases, and carry gold labels
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (there are none to simulate here beyond
      the review outcome)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels: accuracy, a majority-label baseline, per-class F1 via
      `per_class_metrics`, and selective coverage/accuracy/risk via `evaluate_selective`; the issue
      names no model baseline of its own
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below)

## Acceptance criteria (issue #20)

  15 passed

  byte-for-byte identical to run 1

$ pytest -q         # full suite, Python 3.14, foreground, under the shared heavy-job slot
  1696 passed, 3 skipped in ~82s
$ uv venv --python 3.10 <scratch>/venv310 && uv pip install -e ".[dev]"

  wrote 40 examples, 38 labels, 40 responses  — byte-identical to the 3.14 run (diff -rq: no output)

  15 passed
```

### Numbers this recipe reports

- Fixtures: 40 total — 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`. Gold-label balance: `validation`
  supports 7 / contradicts 5 / unresolved 7; `test` supports 6 / contradicts 6 / unresolved 7.
- Confidence threshold chosen on `validation` (`target_accuracy=1.0`): **0.4000**. Validation:
  17 of 19 accepted, 17/17 right among accepted (one wrong example, `v16-low-confidence-wrong`,
  and one correct example, `v08-weaker`, are excluded).
- Majority-label baseline, chosen on `validation` (`supports`): validation accuracy 0.3684, test
  accuracy 0.3158 — versus this recipe's raw `test` accuracy of 0.9474.
- `test`: 17 of 19 accepted by the rule, 16/17 right among accepted. Per-class F1 (`test`):
  `supports` 0.923 (precision 0.857, recall 1.000, support 6), `contradicts` 0.909 (precision
  1.000, recall 0.833, support 6), `unresolved` 1.000 (precision 1.000, recall 1.000, support 7).
- Selective prediction (`test`, threshold 0.4000 frozen): coverage 0.8947 (17/19), accuracy among
  answered 0.9412, **risk 0.0588 (non-zero, from `t16-confident-wrong`)**.
- Live-mode request count: exactly 40 (one per fixture example, each decided once and cached —
  printed by the notebook itself in the `measured` cell: "distinct passages decided this run (1
  request each in live mode): 40"), hence the README's `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=40` note.

## Decisions

- The use case's own fallback outcome, `unresolved`, is a real class, not an unconditional-review
  fallback: every option is one Python is willing to report, so `classify`'s only review branch is
  the confidence gate, and the evaluation stays on `evaluate_selective` (per the brief guidance, no
  `evaluate_outcomes` distinction to draw here).
- "Candidate sets are assembled by Python and shown to the reader" (issue acceptance criterion) is
  satisfied by the fixed, Python-built three-option `OPTIONS` tuple (there is one passage and one
  claim per example, not a list of candidate passages to select among); this matches the brief
  guidance's reading of recipe 20 as structurally close to recipe 01 (a plain three/four-way
  `Choice` with a confidence-only review branch), not the candidate-shortlist pattern of recipes
  08/11/17/18.
- Added a majority-label baseline (chosen on `validation`, never `test`) that the rule's raw
  accuracy must clearly beat, printed in its own evaluation cell before the per-class metrics.
- The weaker/stronger hard case is split into two paired fixtures: a passage that only supports a
  *narrower* version of the claim is `unresolved` (it does not settle the broader claim as
  literally asked), while a passage that proves a *strictly stronger* claim is `supports` (it
  logically entails the weaker claim asked about). Both are named in the option description for
  `supports` and discussed explicitly in the notebook.

## Unfinished / out of scope

- `README.md`'s generated catalog regions are not touched by this PR; `Catalog (README is
  current)` is expected red until the integration worker updates this branch and runs
  `tools/render_catalog.py`, per the generated-README exception.

title: Recipe 16: Discord moderation triage
body:
Closes #16

## What this adds

`recipes/16-discord-moderation-triage/`: a Level 2 `Choice` recipe that triages fabricated Discord
messages against a supplied community rule into `allowed`, the explicit uncertain outcome
`review_needed`, or `potentially_violating`, then turns the category and its confidence into one
of four simulated moderation actions (`ignore`, `warn`, `hide`, `escalate`) through

`test`, 2 `demo`) exercise the hard cases the issue names: sarcasm, a message that quotes or
reports someone else's abusive words, borderline banter, and a benign message with a trigger
word. Evaluation reports a confusion matrix, the cost of a false allow discussed separately from a
false flag, and selective coverage/accuracy/risk via `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes`
(landed on `main` in #160 while this recipe was being built; used directly, no local workaround
needed).

  (`Catalog` excepted, see above)

## Decisions

- **Action mapping.** `allowed` -> `ignore` (no side effect, so it is final whatever the
  confidence, per CONTRIBUTING.md section 4's low-confidence-fallback-with-no-side-effect
  clause). A flagged category (`review_needed`/`potentially_violating`) below the confidence gate
  -> `escalate` (`ReviewQueue`), whichever of the two it is. Above the gate: `review_needed` ->
  `warn`, `potentially_violating` -> `hide` (`ActionLog`). One confidence gate, selected on the
  *gated* subset of `validation` only (answers whose raw choice is not `allowed`), since `allowed`
  is never gated — reusing every validation answer, `allowed` included, would let ungated
  messages set a threshold for messages the rule does gate.
- **Selective metrics.** `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes` is used directly (it landed
  on `main` via #160 partway through building this recipe); no local `summarize_outcomes` was
  needed.
- **False allow / false flag as the central lesson.** `allowed` bypasses the confidence gate
  structurally, so a confident wrong `allowed` (`t15-false-allow`, confidence 0.7000, gold
  `review_needed`) is a mistake no amount of gate-tuning catches. Contrasted with a confident
  wrong `potentially_violating` (`t17-false-flag`, confidence 0.7750, gold `allowed`) that clears
  the gate anyway. These are the two wrong, answered `test` examples driving the non-zero test
  risk (0.1333); `v07-quoted-abuse` (validation's wrong, gated example at confidence 0.6700) is
  what the confidence gate is chosen to exclude, making the `validation` selection non-vacuous.
- **Action vocabulary, not "review".** This cookbook's lexicon convention names a confidence-gate
  escape hatch "review"; the issue's own build notes specify the action set `ignore`/`warn`/
  `hide`/`escalate` directly, and `escalate` (into `ReviewQueue`) is used verbatim rather than
  renamed to match other recipes' "review" naming, since the brief is explicit about the four
  action names.
- **No shared-package gap encountered.** `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes` (needed for
  a rule whose review branch is more than the confidence gate) merged while this recipe was being
  built, so none of the earlier recipes' local-workaround pattern was needed.

## Numbers

  printed as 0.7600 (exact float `0.7599999999999998`, `v13-violating-harass`'s own confidence).

title: Recipe 14: Source span selection
body:
Closes #14

## What this adds

`recipes/14-source-span-selection/`: a `Choice` recipe where Python extracts candidate spans
from a fabricated purchase document (sentences that might name the supplier), assigns each an
identifier and character offsets, and builds the option set per document from those span ids
plus the shared fallback `not_stated`. Jev picks the span (or `not_stated`); Python returns the
exact source text of a confident pick by slicing the document at its recorded offsets, reports
`not_stated` as a final result whatever its confidence (no stored text to protect, no side
effect), and sends anything else below a `validation`-chosen threshold to `review`.

- `helpers.py`: `build_state`, `build_questions(fields)` (per-document criteria — a
  consequence recipe 07's per-word sense inventory has for its options), `span_text`,
  `spans_by_id`, the rule `select_span` (three outcomes: `supported`, `not_stated`, `review`),
  `matches_gold` (raw-choice correctness) and `is_correct` (rule-outcome correctness).
- `build_fixtures.py`: 40 fabricated purchase documents (19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`),
  spans located by `str.index` so a typo can't silently produce the wrong offset.
- `tests/test_helpers.py` (25 tests) and `tests/test_build_fixtures.py` (3 tests, copied from
  `recipes/_template/tests/test_build_fixtures.py`).
- `notebook.ipynb`, `README.md`.

## Decisions

- **`evaluate_outcomes`, not a recipe-local `summarize_outcomes`.** #160 (shared
  `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes`) merged to `main` before this branch was pushed,
  so this recipe uses it directly rather than recipe 08's local `OutcomeSummary` pattern — no
  recipe-local helper of that shape exists here.
- **State carries only the sliced span text, by id; criteria carry the ids with no
  description.** The candidate spans' content is the thing being judged, so it goes in `state`
  (`{"spans": {id: text}}`); the option identifiers are bare (`None` description), since their
  meaning is already given by the matching id in `state`. A document with zero candidate spans
  gets a one-option `Choice` (`not_stated` only, confidence always 1.0 by the published
  formula) rather than being filtered out — `v17`/`t15` exercise this.
- **Correctness is checked by substring, not by span id.** `matches_gold`/`is_correct` check
  whether the *returned text* contains the gold supplier name, so a document that states the
  supplier in two spans (`v12`, `v13`, `t10`, `t11`) has no single "right" id — either
  qualifying span counts. This is the recipe's answer to the issue's "claim supported by two
  spans" hard case.
- **`not_stated` is final whatever its confidence**, per CONTRIBUTING.md section 4 (updated by
  #162, merged before this branch pushed): a low-confidence fallback may be delivered as a
  final result when choosing it has no side effect. There is no stored span text a confidence
  check could protect for `not_stated`, so it is never gated — the same reasoning recipe 08
  uses for `no_match`.
- **The threshold's selection pool excludes `not_stated` raw picks**, the same exclusion
  recipe 08 applies to `no_match`: feeding an un-gated branch's confidence into
  `select_confidence_threshold` would tune a gate the rule does not have.
- **Validation numbers print `{selection}{check}`** (both labels) in this offline run, per the
  `docs/recipe-template.md` bullet added by #162.
- **`not_stated`-vs-named handling is reported with `confusion_matrix`/`per_class_metrics`**
  on a fixed two-class label (`not_stated`, `named`), not a per-document confusion matrix
  (span ids aren't a shared label space across documents) — this is how "correct handling of
  `not_stated`" is reported separately from exact-match accuracy.

## Numbers

- Fixtures: 40 documents total — 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo` (never scored). 38
  labels. 39 distinct responses (the two documents with no candidate spans at all ask the same
  empty-candidate question and legitimately share one response).
- Threshold (chosen on `validation`, `target_accuracy=1.0`, over 15 named raw picks, 1 of them
  wrong): **0.6400**.
- `validation`: raw-choice accuracy 18/19 = 0.9474; rule outcomes 9 `supported` / 6 `review` /
  4 `not_stated`; `evaluate_outcomes` coverage 0.6842, accuracy **1.0000**, risk **0.0000**.
- `test`: raw-choice accuracy 16/19 = 0.8421; rule outcomes 6 `supported` / 9 `review` / 4
  `not_stated`; `evaluate_outcomes` coverage 0.5263, accuracy **0.8000**, risk **0.2000**
  (non-zero, from two different un-caught mistakes: `t09`, a near-miss decoy confident enough
  to clear the gate; `t14`, a wrong `not_stated` pick the gate is never applied to at all).
  `t07` is wrong but low-confidence and *is* caught (reviewed).
- `not_stated` vs. named (`test`, raw choice): `not_stated` precision 0.750, recall 1.000,
  support 3; `named` precision 1.000, recall 0.938, support 16.
- Request count: 39 distinct questions (one request each in live mode; the live-mode budget
  note in the README says to raise `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` to at least 39).

## How it was verified

All commands from the repository root, Linux, no `.env`, no API key, `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE` unset,
default service tier, under the shared `HEAVY.lock` for every heavy step, in the foreground:

```
uv venv --python 3.14 .venv && uv pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt

python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/14-source-span-selection
  -> recipes/14-source-span-selection: fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/14-source-span-selection -q            -> 28 passed
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/14-source-span-selection   -> exit 0, run twice,
  byte-identical (diff -q clean)
python tools/check_hygiene.py recipes/14-source-span-selection/notebook.ipynb
  -> Hygiene check passed: 1 file(s) scanned.
ruff check .                                           -> All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                                  -> all files already formatted
grep -rn TODO recipes/14-source-span-selection          -> nothing (exit 1)
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/14-source-span-selection --body-file pr-body.txt
  -> scope ok: recipe pull request for #14 (14-source-span-selection): 9 changed paths

# full suite, OMP/MKL/OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2, nice -n 10 timeout 1500, under HEAVY.lock
python -m pytest -q    -> 1709 passed, 3 skipped in 107.91s
  (the 3 skips are typesafe_sdk/pre-commit not installed, pre-existing and unrelated)
```

`python tools/render_catalog.py` was **not** run (recipe builders never run it).

## Recipe checklist

  recipe folder; the generated README regions are added later by the integration worker)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` — not this branch's job; see

- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions (see README "Switch to live")
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which
  mode it ran in (`run_header`, and the "What was and was not measured" cell)
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference

  decoy, a supplier named in two spans, no supplier at all), and carry gold labels

  calls anything real)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels: exact-match accuracy (raw and gated) and `not_stated`
  handling, both from `helpers.select_span`'s own outcomes, never reimplemented inline
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below)

### Issue #14 acceptance criteria

- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, outputs committed (executed twice, byte-identical)
- [x] Live mode opt-in, same question definitions (README "Switch to live")
- [x] Fixtures synthetic, hard cases named in the build notes present, gold labels, fixture
  validator passes
- [x] Every response records provenance (`synthetic`); notebook states its mode (`run_header`)
- [x] Evaluation: exact match on supplier name (raw-choice accuracy + `evaluate_outcomes`) and
  correct handling of `not_stated` (`confusion_matrix`/`per_class_metrics` on the
  `not_stated`-vs-named split)
- [x] Candidate sets assembled by Python and shown to the reader (the "Python has" / "Jev sees"
  cell in "The state")
- [x] The review outcome is exercised by several fixtures (6 on `validation`, 9 on `test`) and
  reported separately from `supported`/`not_stated`
- [x] No statement about Jev's quality, latency or cost without recorded live inference; every
  synthetic-run metric is labelled `(a pipeline check, not a Jev result)`, and every
  `validation` number additionally carries `(a selection step, not a reported result)`
- [x] README states what the recipe teaches, how to run it, what was and was not measured live

  (expected red until integration)

`Catalog (README is current)` is expected red until the integration worker regenerates the root

## Anything I was unsure about

first push): `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes` and the `{selection}{check}` /
