title: Recipe 13: Candidate rewrite selection
body:
Closes #13

## What this adds

Recipe 13, "Candidate rewrite selection" (`recipes/13-candidate-rewrite-selection/`): a `Choice`
over four Python-built options -- `candidate_1`, `candidate_2`, `candidate_3`, and the explicit
fallback `no_suitable_rewrite` -- that chooses among three fixed, fabricated candidate rewrites
of one sentence (never generated by a text model) and keeps the original sentence unchanged when
none of the three both preserves its meaning and matches the requested tone.

- **The question.** One `Choice` question, `rewrite`, instructing Jev to pick the identifier of
  whichever candidate both keeps the original sentence's meaning intact and matches the
  requested tone, or `no_suitable_rewrite` if none of the three does both. The state carries the
  original sentence, the requested tone, and the three candidates under their fixed position
  names; an `item_id` bookkeeping field stays in Python and never reaches the model.
- **Option-order design decision.** `backends.md` notes a `Choice`'s option order is part of its
  replay key, and S07 item 8 documents jev-1.13's lean toward whichever option comes first. This
  recipe fixes the option order (`candidate_1`, `candidate_2`, `candidate_3`,
  `no_suitable_rewrite`, every request) rather than shuffling it per request -- shuffling would
  change the replay key every time and make nothing replayable offline -- and instead
  deliberately varies *which* candidate occupies which position across the fixture set, so the
  correct candidate (when one exists) sits at every one of the three positions across different
  items, and several items have no correct candidate at all. The notebook's "The questions"
  section explains this explicitly.
- **Python's part (`helpers.py`).** `select_rewrite` returns a confident candidate's own text,
  keeps the original sentence unchanged as a final `no_suitable_rewrite`/`kept_original` result
  whatever its confidence (CONTRIBUTING.md's "a low-confidence fallback option may be delivered
  as a final result... but only when choosing it triggers no side effect" -- keeping the
  sentence as written is exactly that), and sends anything else below the confidence gate to an
  explicit `review` outcome. `tests/test_helpers.py` (19 tests) checks the rule at the confidence
  boundary, for a confident and a low-confidence answer at every one of the three candidate
  positions, for `no_suitable_rewrite` at both a high and a low confidence (so it is never
  gated), the inclusive threshold boundary, the out-of-range `ValueError`, that the state hides
  `item_id`, that every fixture's replay key matches the current question, that the stored
  answers are not all right, and -- the stronger guard the lexicon lessons ask for -- that at
  least one wrong answer is at or above the frozen confidence gate on `test` specifically (not
  just "some wrong answer exists somewhere").
- **Fixtures.** 40 examples: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo` (`fixtures/inputs.jsonl`,
  `labels.jsonl`, `responses.json`, all synthetic). One wrong answer sits in `validation` itself
  (`v06-sympathetic-wrong`, a refund-refusal rewrite read as acceptably sympathetic when it is
  actually flat); `test` carries three more, each wrong in a different way (confident-through-the-gate,
  confident-through-the-ungated-fallback, caught-by-the-gate). `build_fixtures.py` follows
  `recipes/_template/build_fixtures.py`'s separation of inputs/labels generation from responses
  generation verbatim, and `tests/test_build_fixtures.py` ships the refusal/separation/byte-identity
  guard tests.
- **Evaluation.** The confidence gate is chosen on `validation` with
  `select_confidence_threshold(target_accuracy=1.0)` over the real-candidate-only matches (the
  `no_suitable_rewrite` answers are excluded from that selection, since the rule never gates
  them), then frozen and reported on `test`: top-1 accuracy, a confusion matrix, per-option
  precision/recall/f1 (including `no_suitable_rewrite`'s own), and selective coverage/accuracy/risk
  from `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)` -- not `evaluate_selective`,
  because the rule's fallback branch is never gated on confidence.

## Numbers (from the committed synthetic run)

- Confidence gate (chosen on `validation`, frozen before `test`): **0.2800**
- `validation` (19 examples): accepted 9, review 3, kept_original 7; top-1 accuracy 0.9474;
  `evaluate_outcomes`: answered 16/19 (coverage 0.8421), accuracy 1.0000, **risk 0.0000** (a
  real, non-vacuous selection: 3 items were actually routed to review to get there, not zero)
- `test` (19 examples): accepted 10, review 3, kept_original 6; top-1 accuracy 0.8421;
  `evaluate_outcomes`: answered 16/19 (coverage 0.8421), accuracy 0.8750, **risk 0.1250** (non-zero,
  as the brief requires)
- `no_suitable_rewrite` per-option: precision 0.8333, recall 0.8333 (support 6)
- Live request count: exactly 40 (one per fixture example, each decided once); README tells the
  reader to raise `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` to at least 40 before running live (default
  budget is 25)

## Decisions

- **Candidate identifiers are positions, not names.** Unlike recipe 08's FAQ identifiers (stable
  names describing fixed content), `candidate_1`/`candidate_2`/`candidate_3` name *positions*
  Python assigns; the text at each position changes every item. Each option's description is
  therefore the same three sentences with only the position name substituted -- there is nothing
  stable to say about a position ahead of time. This is a deliberate, documented departure from
  recipe 08's per-option-description pattern, not an oversight.
- **`item_id` passed to `select_rewrite` is `fields["item_id"]`** (an `R####` bookkeeping code),
  matching recipes 08/09's convention, not the fixture's own `id` string (`v06-sympathetic-wrong`
  etc.), which is used only in prose and as the dict key for `demo`/example lookups in the
  notebook.
- **`jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes` used instead of a local `summarize_outcomes`.**
  The brief's guidance called for a local helper pending #160; #160 merged into `main` while this
  branch was in progress (before any push), so this PR integrates that `main` and uses the shared
  `evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)` directly -- no local `OutcomeSummary`/`summarize_outcomes`
  exists in `helpers.py`.
- **README install line and "Pull request rules" wording follow #162**, merged into `main` while
  this branch was also in progress (again before any push): `pip install -e ".[dev]"` for the
  offline/test commands, with the `.[ml]` + constraints-file install called out separately only
  for reproducing notebook outputs byte for byte; the "Pull request rules" paragraph matches the
  scaffolder's current (post-#162) wording.
- **`docs/glossary.md`'s new "gold label" entry (also from #162) is linked** on the term's first
  notebook prose use. The lexicon lessons ask for glossary links on "business threshold,
  confidence gate, review, gold label, coverage, risk, selective prediction" generally, but
  `docs/glossary.md` currently defines anchors only for "gold label", "accuracy" and "threshold"
  (plus the original state/question/Choice/etc. set) -- not for "confidence gate", "review",
  "coverage", "risk" or "selective prediction" specifically, nor for the exact phrase "business
  threshold". Those terms are defined inline in prose, the way recipes 08/09/10 already do, with
  no dead link. This is the same gap issue #164 (template/docs follow-ups) already tracks; I did
  not add glossary entries myself, since `docs/glossary.md` is shared code outside this recipe's
  allowed path.
- **Review-round guidance applied before opening:** the one `in`-based reason-string assertion
  was tightened to an exact `== "confidence below the threshold"` comparison; no test compares a
  `helpers.X[label]` lookup to itself; every validation/test aggregate number in the notebook
  carries `{selection}`/`{check}`; no sentence attributes behaviour to Jev from the synthetic
  answers.

## Commands run (all pass; see below for render_catalog, expected red)

```
ruff check .                                            # All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                                   # 138 files already formatted
pytest                                                   # 1700 passed, 3 skipped (pre-existing, not mine)
pytest recipes/13-candidate-rewrite-selection            # 19 passed (also verified on a Python 3.10 venv)
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/13-candidate-rewrite-selection
                                                          # fixtures valid (mode replay)
python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/13-candidate-rewrite-selection
                                                          # executed twice; second run changed nothing (git diff --stat empty)
python tools/check_hygiene.py                            # Hygiene check passed: 196 file(s) scanned.
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/13-candidate-rewrite-selection --body-file pr-body.txt
                                                          # scope ok: recipe pull request for #13 (13-candidate-rewrite-selection): 9 changed paths
python tools/render_catalog.py --check                   # README.md is out of date (EXPECTED: integration worker's job, not mine)
```

`build_fixtures.py` also verified byte-identical between Python 3.14 and 3.10.

title: Recipe 12: Thesaurus word selection
body:
Closes #12

## What this adds

`recipes/12-thesaurus-word-selection/`: a `Choice` recipe that picks a context-appropriate
synonym from a small candidate list Python assembles fresh for each sentence (not a table
shared by every sentence that uses the same target word), plus a shared fallback,
`keep_original`, for a sentence where none of the candidates preserve the word's meaning.

- **The question.** One `Choice` named `synonym`, instructions `"The word {word!r} appears in
  the sentence below. Choose the option that could replace {word!r} without changing the
  sentence's meaning. If none of the supplied words preserve the meaning, choose
  'keep_original'."` The option set is `candidate_options(word, candidates)`
  (`helpers.py`): this sentence's own 3 candidate synonyms (each with a short, context-free
  dictionary gloss from `SYNONYM_DEFINITIONS`), in the order the fixture gives them, then
  `keep_original` last. Because the candidate list is assembled per sentence rather than per
  word, two sentences about the same target word can be offered different candidates, and the
  replay key (option order is part of it) follows the sentence, never the word: editing one
  sentence's candidates in `build_fixtures.py` invalidates only that sentence's stored response,
  unlike recipe 07's per-word sense inventory, where changing one word's senses invalidates
  every sentence that uses it.
- **The fallback's consequence.** Unlike a Choice option that only ever means "the model could
  not decide" (recipe 07's `unclear`), `keep_original` is a real, final answer: it is the
  correct, scorable outcome whenever a fixture's gold set says no candidate fits, it triggers no
  side effect of its own, and `helpers.resolve` holds it to exactly the same confidence gate as
  every other option rather than routing it to review automatically. `tests/test_helpers.py`
  checks this for every kind of option, including a confident `keep_original` reaching
  `accepted`.
- **Python's rule (`helpers.resolve`).** Accepts the chosen option only when it was one Jev was
  actually offered (defensive membership check; unreachable through replay, since the backend
  restricts answers to the question's own options, but kept per the Noul-pattern decision that a
  rule keeps a defensive membership branch) *and* its `confidence` is at or above a threshold
  chosen on `validation` (`select_confidence_threshold(..., target_accuracy=1.0)`) and frozen on
  `test`. Everything else goes to the `review` outcome, reason string exactly `"confidence below
  the threshold"` or `"not a supplied option"`.
- **Evaluation**, exactly the two numbers the issue names, plus the standard selective-prediction
  triple:
  - share of selections inside each sentence's own acceptable set (gold is a list, since more
    than one synonym can fit; no helper in `jev_cookbook.evaluation` computes set-membership
    accuracy, so this is a one-line manual comparison, computed the same way on `validation`
    (selection label) and `test` (check label));
  - precision/recall/F1 of `keep_original` as its own class, via
    `jev_cookbook.evaluation.per_class_metrics` on a derived two-class relabelling
    (`keep_original` vs `other`) — reported separately, on the raw choice, before the confidence
    gate, per the issue's "reported separately" wording;
  - coverage, accuracy and risk of the frozen rule's own accept/review decisions on `test`, via
    `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)` (this recipe's rule has a
    review branch beyond the confidence gate, so `evaluate_selective` would silently disagree
    with `resolve` the moment the defensive branch ever fired — see `docs/evaluation.md`,
    "Selective prediction", and the `docs/recipe-template.md` section #160 added on `main` while
    this recipe was being built).

### Fixture counts and the numbers they produce

43 examples total: 20 `validation`, 20 `test`, 3 `demo` (never scored). 40 labelled, across four
target words (`happy`, `big`, `quick`, `angry`), 3 candidates each. `validation` carries exactly
one wrong stored answer, `v05-happy-wrong`, at a moderate confidence (0.55 → confidence 0.40);
excluding it from the accepted set is what the threshold search on `validation` actually has to
do (non-vacuous selection), landing the frozen threshold at **0.7333**. `test` carries two wrong
stored answers: `t05-quick-wrong` (confidence 0.80, above the frozen threshold, so the rule
accepts it anyway) and `t03-angry-nomatch` (confidence 0.2267, below the threshold, so the gate
catches it). `tests/test_helpers.py::test_a_wrong_test_answer_clears_the_frozen_confidence_threshold`
recomputes the threshold the same way the notebook does and asserts this directly, rather than
only commenting on it.

Numbers from the committed (synthetic) run, every one labelled `check` in the notebook:

- selections inside the acceptable set — validation: 19/20 (0.9500, `selection` label); test:
  18/20 (0.9000, `check` label)
- accepted by the rule — validation: 15/20, all 15 right; test: 15/20, 14 right
- `keep_original` — support 4/20, precision 1.0000, recall 0.7500, F1 0.8571 (the one miss,
  `t03-angry-nomatch`, is also one of the five sentences the confidence gate separately sends to
  review, for its own reason — the two mechanisms catch it differently)
- `evaluate_outcomes` on test: answered 15/20 (coverage 0.7500), accuracy 0.9333, **risk 0.0667**
  (non-zero, driven by `t05-quick-wrong`)

### Request count

43 in live mode (one per fixture example, each decided once via a cache keyed by example id, the
`demo` examples included) — above the live backend's default budget of 25, so the README tells a
live reader to set `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=43` or higher first.

## Decisions a later builder should know about

- **Gold labels are lists**, not single strings: `labels.jsonl`'s `label` is the set of every
  option that preserves the sentence's meaning (one candidate, several, or `["keep_original"]`
  when none do). This is allowed by `docs/fixtures.md` ("`label` is any JSON value except
  `null`"), but it means `jev_cookbook.evaluation.accuracy` cannot be used directly against it
  (it expects exact equality); the "share inside the acceptable set" number above is a one-line
  manual membership check instead, explained in the notebook as a deliberate, not-a-gap choice.
- **`keep_original` is not sent to review automatically.** This recipe's build notes ask for a
  fallback outcome, and the obvious copy from recipe 07 (`unclear`, always reviewed) does not fit:
  here the fallback is itself frequently the one *correct* answer. I resolved this by holding
  `keep_original` to the same confidence gate as every other option, and said so explicitly in
  both `helpers.py`'s docstring and the notebook's "Python's part" section, so a later recipe
  that copies this shape does not accidentally also copy the always-review behaviour that does
  not apply here.
- **Candidates are per-sentence, not per-word.** `build_questions(word, candidates)` takes the
  candidate list as an argument built directly from each fixture row's own `fields["candidates"]`,
  rather than looking it up from a shared per-word table the way recipe 07's `SENSE_INVENTORY`
  does. This is the "per-item option sets" pattern the brief asked for; the replay-key
  consequence is explained in the notebook's "The questions" section and above.
- **`evaluate_outcomes` landed on `main` (#160) while this recipe was in progress.** I merged
  that `main` (fast-forward, `c61af62` → `0d8c95d`) before writing the evaluation section and
  used `evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct)` directly; no local `summarize_outcomes` workaround
  was needed or written.

## How it was verified

All commands run from a clean `uv venv --python 3.14 .venv`,
`uv pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`, from this branch's head:

```

  -> wrote 43 examples, 40 labels, 43 responses

  -> recipes/12-thesaurus-word-selection: fixtures valid (mode replay)

  -> 23 passed

  -> 12-thesaurus-word-selection: executed notebook.ipynb offline (both times)
  -> git diff --stat notebook.ipynb empty between the two runs
ruff check .
  -> All checks passed!
ruff format --check .
  -> 137 files already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py
  -> Hygiene check passed: 195 file(s) scanned.
python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/12-thesaurus-word-selection --body-file <this file>
  -> scope ok: recipe pull request for #12 (12-thesaurus-word-selection): 9 changed paths

`python tools/render_catalog.py` was **not** run, and `README.md` was **not** hand-edited:

title: Recipe 15: Sensitive text triage
body:
Closes #15

## What this adds

`recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage/`: a Level 2 `Noul` recipe that flags synthetic documents
which may contain personal information so a simulated review queue can prioritize redaction
checks. Before any document reaches Jev, Python runs a deterministic candidate-span scan
(`helpers.find_candidate_spans`: email-, phone-, and street-address-shaped substrings) and shows
it to the reader. Jev answers one proposition per document ("this document may contain personal
information about a real, identifiable person"). Python then applies a three-outcome rule
(`helpers.triage`): a business threshold (`select_threshold`, objective `f1`, chosen on
`validation`) decides `flagged`/`cleared`; an independent confidence gate
(`select_confidence_threshold`, `min_coverage=0.80`, also chosen on `validation`) sends a
document to `review` instead of a forced guess whenever its confidence (`noul_confidence`,
`|2p - 1|`) is too low. A `jev_cookbook.simulation.ReviewQueue` is ordered by the stored
probability, highest first, per the issue's build note. The evaluation reports precision/recall/
f1 at the business threshold, the confidence gate's own coverage-vs-accuracy curve against the
ungated rule, and `recall_at_budget` (a fixed review-capacity framing) for both splits.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage/` (nothing else; the generated
      README regions are regenerated separately by the integration worker)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` -- **not run by this builder**,
      per the generated-README exception (CONTRIBUTING.md); `Catalog (README is current)` is
      expected red on this PR until the integration worker runs
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage/`
      paths, every mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change, no rename or deletion out of scope
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network (outputs committed; two
      runs of `tools/execute_notebook.py` are byte-identical)
- [x] Live path is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`) and uses the same question
      definitions as the offline path
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states its mode
      in the first cell's `run_header` output and again in "What was and was not measured"
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost anywhere in the folder; every number is
      labelled as a pipeline check (offline) and/or a selection step (validation)
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic (52 fabricated documents: 25 `validation`, 25 `test`, 2 `demo`),
      include the hard cases named in the issue's build notes, and carry gold labels for every
      scored example
- [x] Python owns every side effect: `triage` only decides an outcome, nothing is redacted, and
      the README/notebook say so plainly; `ReviewQueue.submit` only records, never executes
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels with `jev_cookbook.evaluation`; this recipe names no prior
      baseline (the issue does not name one)
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below)

## How it was verified

All commands below were run in `/workspace/worktrees/recipe-15` against this head, with
`uv venv --python 3.14 .venv` + `uv pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`
for the 3.14 venv, and `uv venv --python 3.10 .venv310` + `uv pip install -e ".[dev]"` for the
3.10 venv. Heavy jobs (both venv installs, both notebook executions, the full suite) ran one at a
time under the repository's shared `HEAVY.lock`, in the foreground.

```
python recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage/build_fixtures.py
  -> wrote 52 examples, 50 labels, 52 responses

python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage
  -> recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage: fixtures valid (mode replay)      [3.14 and 3.10]

pytest recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage
  -> 29 passed                                                            [3.14 and 3.10]

ruff check recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage        -> All checks passed!
ruff format --check recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage -> 6 files already formatted

python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/15-sensitive-text-triage   (run twice)
  -> both runs exit 0; the two notebook.ipynb files are byte-identical (`cmp`)

python tools/check_hygiene.py
  -> Hygiene check passed: 186 file(s) scanned.

pytest   (full suite, repository root, 3.14 venv)
  -> 1684 passed, 3 skipped in ~85-100s
     (the 3 skips are pre-existing and unrelated to this recipe: no typesafe_sdk installed,
     no pre-commit/local ruff binary -- confirmed by rerunning with -rs)

python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head HEAD \
    --branch recipe/15-sensitive-text-triage --body-file pr-body.md
  -> scope ok: recipe pull request for #15 (15-sensitive-text-triage): 9 changed paths
```

`python tools/render_catalog.py` was **not** run, on purpose (see checklist above).

## Decisions

- **Candidate-span scan is Python-only context, never sent to Jev.** `helpers.find_candidate_spans`
  (email/phone/street regexes) is shown to the reader next to every document in "The state" and
  "One answer up close", satisfying the issue's "Candidate sets are assembled by Python and shown
  to the reader" criterion, but `build_state` passes on the document text alone -- the scan is a
  heuristic that gets fooled in both directions (a benign tracking number that looks like a phone
  number; a narrative PII mention with no matching token at all), which is the point: it motivates
  asking Jev a judgment rather than trusting the pattern match.
- **The review queue is built with both `flagged` and `review` documents, ordered by `noul`
  descending**, not only `review` documents (contrast recipes 02/10): the issue's build note asks
  for the queue to be ordered by the noul value so the most-likely-to-contain-PII documents surface
  first for a redaction check, and both outcomes need a person to look at the document (one to
  redact, one to decide what it even is) -- only `cleared` documents are excluded, and the README
  and notebook both say plainly that clearing a document is a prioritization choice, not proof it
  contains no personal information.
- **`recall_at_budget` is reported as a second, independent metric**, not folded into the
  three-outcome rule's own accounting: it answers "if a redaction team only has capacity to review
  the top `BUDGET` documents in `noul` order, what share of the real positives would they reach,"
  which is a property of the ranking alone and ignores the business threshold and the `review`
  outcome entirely. `BUDGET = 10` (of 25 per split) is a fixed Python constant with no learned
  selection step.
- **The signature hard case is an adversarial document, not a "fluent wrong answer".** One
  document per split embeds an instruction trying to steer the triage into clearing it, immediately
  followed by a real name, phone number and address; its stored probability is confidently low
  (noul 0.12/0.13, confidence 0.76/0.74), so the confidence gate -- which measures distance from an
  even split, not correctness -- does not catch it, and the document is wrongly `cleared` rather
  than reviewed. This ties directly to S07 (adversarial content) and is a stronger, more
  on-theme lesson for a trust-and-security recipe than a confident false positive would have been:
  the triage can be made to silently drop a document that genuinely contains personal information.
  Both splits also carry a `-lookalike`/`-miss` document (a tracking reference formatted like a
  phone number, and a business-rule-alone miss just under the threshold) that the gate *does*
  catch, so the notebook shows both what the gate buys and what it cannot buy.
- **`test` is not a mirror of `validation`.** The two splits use different documents and a
  different count/shape of near-threshold mistakes (`validation` has one caught error,
  `test` has two), so precision/recall/f1, coverage, accuracy and risk are all genuinely different
  between the splits (0.929/0.929/0.929 vs 0.917/0.846/0.880; coverage 0.840 vs 0.880); the
  "Unlike `validation`, `test` is not a close echo of it" markdown cell spells out why.
- **Vocabulary follows the Wave 2 lexicon** (business threshold; confidence gate, never
  "certainty"; the `review` outcome's reason string is exactly `"confidence below the threshold"`;
  gold label, coverage, risk all defined on first appearance); validation numbers in this
  synthetic run print `{selection}{check}` concatenated, test numbers print only `{check}`.
- **`tests/test_helpers.py` ships `test_stored_answers_are_not_all_right`**, which recomputes the
  business threshold and confidence gate from the committed fixtures the same way the notebook
  does and asserts at least one `test` document clears the gate while still being wrong, so a
  future fixture edit that quietly removes the lesson fails CI rather than only a visual review.
- **No baseline is named by the issue**, so none is reported; the evaluation section says this
  only implicitly by not mentioning one (`jev_cookbook.evaluation` has no catalog of named
  baselines to compare against here).

## Unfinished / open questions

Nothing is unfinished. One thing worth flagging to a reviewer rather than silently deciding:
`recall_at_budget` is a recipe-local addition to the three-path pattern (not previously used by a
merged Noul recipe); if a future shared-helper correction changes its semantics, this recipe's
`BUDGET` cell and its two prose paragraphs would need a re-read against the new docstring.

title: Recipe 17: Passage reranking
body:
Closes #17

## What this adds

`recipes/17-passage-reranking/`: a passage reranker. For each of ten scored queries (five
`validation`, five `test`, four passages each) plus one `demo` query (three passages), Jev
answers one `Score` question per (query, passage) pair against a four-level relevance rubric
(`not_relevant`, `tangential`, `relevant`, `direct`). Python assembles every candidate set, runs
a small lexical word-overlap scorer as the baseline retrieval order, sorts candidates by Jev's
expected score with ties broken by that baseline order, and gates whether a score is confident
enough to act on (`match`/`no_match`/`review`) with a frozen confidence gate selected on
`validation`. The evaluation reports exact-level agreement and mean absolute error against the
human rubric, the frozen gate's coverage/accuracy/risk on `test`, and two ranking metrics --
nDCG and top-1 accuracy -- comparing Jev's reranking against the lexical baseline on every query.

## Decisions

- **Rubric and business cutoff.** Four standalone levels (`not_relevant` 0, `tangential` 1,
  `relevant` 2, `direct` 3); `BUSINESS_CUTOFF = 2` is a fixed `helpers.py` constant, not
  searched for, per the Score-recipe pattern from recipe 03.
- **Ranking order and the confidence gate are deliberately orthogonal.** `rerank` sorts every
  candidate by its expected score, ties broken by the lexical baseline's order, and never looks
  at confidence. Whether to trust and act on a passage's call (`match`/`no_match` vs `review`)
  is a separate function (`classify`). I considered folding confidence into the rank order
  itself (e.g. demoting low-confidence passages) and decided against it: the issue's build notes
  ask for "ties and confidence handled explicitly," and keeping them as two explicit, separately
  testable mechanisms seemed more honest than one rule that conflates "where does this rank" with
  "do we trust this call." The notebook's "Python's part" section says this in prose.
- **Baseline.** `lexical_score`/`baseline_rank` in `helpers.py`: a deliberately dumb word-overlap
  count (no stemming, no synonyms, no weighting), standing in for "the original retrieval order
  from a small lexical scorer written in plain Python" the issue's build notes ask for. Several
  passages are worded as paraphrases to defeat it on purpose (one `validation` query, one `test`
  query), so the baseline-vs-reranked comparison is not vacuous; three of the five queries per
  split leave the baseline already correct, so the comparison is not rigged to always favour
  reranking either.
- **Foundation gap: no "mean over queries" top-k ranking helper.** `jev_cookbook.evaluation` has
  `mean_ndcg` to average `ndcg` over several ranked lists, but nothing equivalent for a top-1 (or
  top-k) ranking metric: `top_k_accuracy` is for a single Choice-style probability distribution
  over one example's options, not a ranked list of per-passage scores over several queries, and
  `recall_at_budget` reports one list at a time with no "mean over queries" counterpart. I added
  `top1_accuracy(queries)` to this recipe's `helpers.py`, with its own tests in
  `tests/test_helpers.py` (a clear winner, a wrong top-scored item, averaging over queries, a
  tied-at-the-top case matching `recall_at_budget`'s own tie rule, and the two error cases). It
  is a thin wrapper around `evaluation.recall_at_budget(relevant, scores, budget=1)` per query,
  averaged, so every actual rule (tie-breaking, what counts as relevant) stays inside the shared,
  tested helper. **This should move into `jev_cookbook.evaluation` itself** (as, say,
  `mean_recall_at_budget` or a dedicated top-k ranking accuracy, the same way `mean_ndcg` sits
  beside `ndcg`) in a foundation pull request; I did not add it there myself, per the recipe
  builder's allowed paths.
- **Sources.** The README's Sources section lists exactly S02/S03/S04/S06, matching the catalog
  row for rank 17. The general Score-recipe guidance (learned from recipe 03) suggests citing S07
  for an adversarial-content fixture; I used an adversarial-style fixture anyway (a passage that
  claims its own relevance without stating anything that answers the query, in `demo` and in
  `test`) because it is a useful hard case on its own terms, but did not add S07 as a numbered
  source, on the explicit instruction that this recipe's sources must equal the catalog row.
- **Lexicon.** Used "business cutoff" (not "business threshold") for the fixed level cutoff, per
  the Wave 1 consistency addendum sent directly to me, which postdates and overrides the wording
  in `RECIPE_BRIEF_GUIDANCE.md`'s own Lexicon section at the time I read it.
- **Non-vacuous gate selection.** `validation` carries one passage (`v03-tangential-wrong`) that
  is wrong at low confidence, so `select_confidence_threshold(target_accuracy=1.0)` has to
  exclude it to reach perfect agreement -- a real choice (gate 0.56, 3 of 20 routed to `review`),
  not one that happens to cover everyone. `test` carries one passage
  (`t06-adversarial-wrong`) that is wrong *and* confident (0.68, above the frozen gate), so
  selective risk on `test` is 0.0556, not zero.

## Numbers (all synthetic; pipeline checks, not Jev results)

- Fixtures: 43 examples total -- 20 `validation` + 20 `test` (5 queries x 4 passages each,
  scored) + 3 `demo` (1 query x 3 passages, never scored). 43 stored responses, 43 requests in
  live mode.
- Confidence gate selected on `validation`: **0.5600**. Validation outcomes: match 10, no_match
  7, review 3 (of 20); exact-level agreement 0.9500; MAE 0.2405 levels.
- Test at the frozen gate: match 11, no_match 7, review 2 (of 20); exact-level agreement 0.9500;
  MAE 0.3585 levels. Selective: coverage 0.9000 (18 of 20), accuracy 0.9444, **risk 0.0556**
  (non-zero).

title: Recipe 18: Duplicate incident matching
body:
Closes #18

## What this adds

`recipes/18-duplicate-incident-matching/`: a `Choice` recipe that matches a new incident ticket
against a shortlist of open incidents Python retrieves, or reports `no_match`.

- **State:** the new ticket's `symptoms` and affected `service`, as two separate fields
  (the use case's own build note). The ticket id stays in Python.
- **Retrieval:** `helpers.shortlist(symptoms)` ranks a fixed pool of 8 open incidents by plain
  word overlap with the new ticket's symptoms (Jaccard similarity over a small stopword-filtered
  token set; ties break on the incident id) and keeps the top 3. It never looks at the affected
  service, on purpose: a textually similar incident on a different service can still be
  retrieved, because telling the two apart is exactly the judgment the question asks Jev to make.
- **Question:** one `Choice`, per ticket, over that ticket's own 3 retrieved candidates plus the
  explicit fallback `no_match`. Each candidate's description carries its own service and
  symptoms; the shared instructions state the matching rule in words (same problem *and* same
  service).
- **Python's rule (`match_incident`):** links a confident real candidate to the new ticket (the
  one outcome with a simulated side effect); reports `no_match` as a final result whatever its
  confidence (no side effect to protect there); sends a candidate outside the retrieved shortlist
  to review as a defensive check; sends a real candidate below the confidence gate to review.
  `helpers.record_resolution` carries out the simulated side effect: a link recorded in a
  `jev_cookbook.simulation.ActionLog` (never executed) or a ticket queued in a `ReviewQueue`.
- **Evaluation:** the confidence gate is chosen on `validation` with
  `select_confidence_threshold` (over the real-candidate matches only, excluding `no_match`,
  which is never gated), frozen, then applied to `test`. `jev_cookbook.evaluation.accuracy`
  reports top-1 match accuracy (raw choice vs. gold label) on both splits; `helpers.summarize_
  outcomes` computes coverage, accuracy and risk directly from the rule's own outcomes, plus a
  false-merge rate scoped to the `linked` outcome alone (the only way the simulated side effect
  can be wrong).

## Decisions

- **`evaluate_outcomes` has not merged (tracked in #160).** Per the recipe brief, selective
  numbers (coverage/accuracy/risk) and the false-merge rate are computed directly from
  `match_incident`'s own outcomes in `helpers.summarize_outcomes`, following the same pattern
  recipe 08's `summarize_outcomes` already uses, and the notebook and `helpers.py` say so. No
  sentinel confidence is ever passed to `select_confidence_threshold` or `evaluate_selective`.
- **Retrieval ignores the affected service by design.** `shortlist` ranks on symptom-text overlap
  alone; filtering by service before Jev ever sees the ticket would remove the exact
  discrimination (same incident vs. similar wording on a different service) this recipe's
  question exists to teach.
- **Shortlist size is fixed at 3** (`SHORTLIST_SIZE` in `helpers.py`), so every question has
  exactly 4 options and the Choice confidence formula is the same `(p_max - 0.25) / 0.75` on
  every ticket.
- **Candidates are recomputed, not stored.** `fields` carries only `ticket_id`, `service` and
  `symptoms`; `shortlist(symptoms)` is deterministic, so the candidate list is recomputed
  wherever it is needed (notebook, tests, `build_fixtures.py`) rather than carried as a second
  piece of state that could drift out of sync with it.
- **Vocabulary and consistency pass.** Built after the Wave 1 consistency review landed in the
  shared recipe-brief guidance (new "Lexicon" section): prose says "confidence gate" (never
  "certainty"), the review outcome's reason string is exactly `"confidence below the threshold"`,
  terms are defined on first prose use, cell ids are semantic, `tests/test_helpers.py` ships
  `test_stored_answers_are_not_all_right` asserting a wrong answer clears the frozen gate, and
  recipe files cite no internal issue numbers (this PR description is not a recipe file, so it
  still names the tracking issue above for the reviewer).

## How it was verified

All commands below were run from a clean `uv venv --python 3.14 .venv` with
`uv pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`, from this branch's head.

title: Recipe 11: Clarification selection
body:
Closes #11

## What this adds

`recipes/11-clarification-selection/`: a `Choice` recipe that selects a useful follow-up
question from a predefined catalog of six entries (`ask_deadline`, `ask_recipient`,
`ask_scope`, `ask_format`, `ask_budget`, `ask_access_level`), each one specific follow-up
question, plus the explicit fallback `no_clarification_needed` for a task description that
already states everything its next step needs. Python owns the catalog, the stored question
text for each entry, and the rule (`select_followup` in `helpers.py`) that asks the stored
question for a confident real match, accepts `no_clarification_needed` as a final result
whatever its confidence (it has no stored question a confidence check could protect, and
triggers no side effect in this recipe), and sends anything else uncertain — including a
defensively-checked option outside the catalog — to an explicit `review` outcome.

### Exact question definition

One `Choice` question, `clarification`, over the state `{"task": <task description text>}`
(the `task_id` stays in Python). Criteria are the six catalog identifiers plus
`no_clarification_needed`, each with a description that says what belongs to it and, for the
two pairs easiest to confuse (a stated recipient vs. a stated, but narrower, access list; a
stated scope vs. a stated, but undetermined, format), what belongs to the neighbouring option
instead. The rule:

- a real catalog option (`ask_*`) at confidence ≥ the frozen confidence gate → `ask`, Python
  returns the stored question text;
- `no_clarification_needed`, at any confidence → `proceed`, Python returns `None` and triggers
  no simulated action (the notebook's "Python's part" section says this explicitly, since the
  issue does not name a side effect to simulate);
- anything else (a real catalog option below the gate, or an option outside the catalog
  entirely — defensive, since `build_questions` never offers one) → `review`, reason string
  exactly `"confidence below the threshold"` for the gated case.

### Fixtures

40 total: 19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo` (never scored). Every `ask_*` option has at
least 2 examples in both `validation` and `test`; `no_clarification_needed` has 3 in
`validation` and 4 in `test`. Hard cases the issue names — a task missing exactly one piece of
information (every `ask_*`-labelled row) and a task missing nothing
(`no_clarification_needed`) — are both represented, and `build_fixtures.py`'s module docstring
and the `ROWS` comments name each deliberately-wrong row and why. All 40 stored answers are
synthetic.

### Threshold and evaluation numbers

Confidence gate chosen on `validation` (`select_confidence_threshold`, over the 16 real-catalog
answers there, excluding `no_clarification_needed`, `target_accuracy=1.0`): **0.3350**, chosen
specifically to exclude the one deliberately-wrong `validation` answer (`v08-scope-wrong`,
confidence 0.3000). Non-vacuous: without that wrong answer the selector would have nothing real
to cut on; with it, `validation` shows a real, non-zero review count (1 of 19).

- `validation` (selection step): accuracy of the selected follow-up 0.9474; ask 15 / review 1 /
  proceed 3 (of 19); outcome summary (rule's own outcomes) coverage 0.9474, accuracy 1.0000,
  risk 0.0000; ask-or-proceed decision accuracy 1.0000.
- `test` (pipeline check): accuracy of the selected follow-up 0.8421; ask 13 / review 1 /
  proceed 5 (of 19); outcome summary coverage 0.9474, accuracy 0.8889, **risk 0.1111**
  (non-zero, from `t09-format-wrong` — a wrong catalog entry the gate lets through at
  confidence 0.4750 — and `t12-budget-wrong` — a wrong, confident `no_clarification_needed`
  the gate never checks); ask-or-proceed decision accuracy 0.9474.

### Request count

40 (one per fixture example; each example decided once and cached, including when it is shown
individually before being scored in its split). The README's live section states this and the
default `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` budget of 25, and tells the reader to raise it to 40.

## Decisions

- **`no_clarification_needed` bypasses the confidence gate entirely, like `no_match` in recipe
  08 and `unclear_request` in recipe 04.** It has no stored payload a confidence check could
  protect (there is nothing to deliver, only a "nothing to ask" signal), and accepting it
  triggers no side effect in this recipe, which the notebook's "Python's part" section states
  explicitly, per the pattern decision that a low-confidence fallback may be final only when it
  triggers no side effect and the notebook says so. `t12-budget-wrong` in the fixtures exercises
  exactly this: a confident, wrong `no_clarification_needed` answer that the rule accepts as
  final anyway.
- **Selective (coverage/accuracy/risk) numbers come from the rule's own outcomes
  (`helpers.summarize_outcomes`), not from `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_selective`.** That
  helper assumes the confidence gate is the rule's only review branch, which is false here
  (`no_clarification_needed` bypasses it). `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes`, the
  shared helper for exactly this case, is still open on `main` as of this branch (PR #160), so
  this recipe computes the summary directly, the same way recipe 08's `summarize_outcomes`
  does. No sentinel confidence (`-1.0`, `0.0`) is ever fed to a selective-prediction helper.
- **Two accuracy numbers, per the issue's acceptance criterion.** "Accuracy of the selected
  follow-up" is top-1 accuracy of the raw `Choice` over all seven options; "accuracy of the
  ask-or-proceed decision" collapses the six `ask_*` options into one "ask" outcome and scores
  only whether the rule's raw choice agreed with the gold label on asking *something* at all,
  versus proceeding. The notebook's per-class cell explains the gap between the two numbers on
  `test` (0.8421 vs. 0.9474): two of the three wrong raw choices still correctly decide that
  something should be asked, even though they name the wrong thing.
- **No simulated side effect is built**, beyond the "ask" / "proceed" / "review" outcome
  itself: the issue's build notes do not name a dry-run preview, queue, or routing table for
  this recipe (unlike recipe 09's folder-placement preview), so none is added.
- **Fixture domain**: short, fabricated office task requests (reports, exports, bookings,
  shared documents) with one of six kinds of information each optionally missing. Chosen so
  each catalog option maps to a concrete, checkable absence in the task text, and so the two
  confusable pairs named above have natural, plausible near-misses to write fixtures for.

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/11-clarification-selection/` (plus the generated README
  regions, not yet regenerated — see below)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` — **not run by this builder**;
  `--check` currently fails (`README.md is out of date`), expected until the integration worker
  updates this branch against current `main` and regenerates it, per CONTRIBUTING.md's
  generated-README exception
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/11-clarification-selection/`
  paths, every entry `A` with mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change, no rename or deletion
  out of scope
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network (outputs committed; ran
  twice, byte-identical)
- [x] Live path is opt-in (`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` + `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`) and uses the same
  question definition
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook's `run_header`
  states which mode ran
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference (none
  recorded here; every number is labelled a pipeline check or a selection step)
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases the issue names, and carry gold labels for
  every scored example
- [x] Python owns every side effect; the one branch that could have one
  (`no_clarification_needed`) triggers none, stated explicitly
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels with `jev_cookbook.evaluation` (`accuracy`,
  `confusion_matrix`, `per_class_metrics`, `select_confidence_threshold`) and the rule's own
  outcomes (`helpers.summarize_outcomes`); the issue names no baseline to compare against
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below)

### Acceptance criteria (issue #11)

- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, no key, no network; outputs committed — verified,
  executed twice, byte-identical
- [x] Live mode opt-in, same question definitions — `tools/execute_notebook.py` strips

title: Evaluation: guard select_confidence_threshold inputs; add evaluate_outcomes
body:
Closes #155

## What this adds

Two changes to `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py`, both scoped to the selective-prediction family
(`selective_curve`, `select_confidence_threshold`, `evaluate_selective`), plus the new
`evaluate_outcomes`:

1. **Confidence is now validated to `[0, 1]`.** `_conf_inputs` (the shared helper behind all
   three existing selective functions) called `_floats(...)` without `unit_interval=True`, so it
   accepted any finite float as a confidence. A rule with an option-based review branch beyond a
   confidence gate (recipe 09's `unsorted`, recipe 07's `unclear`) has no real confidence for the
   answers it rejects outright, and both recipes' reviews (#148, #153) show the sentinel this
   produces (`-1.0`, or a surrogate `0.0`) reaching `select_confidence_threshold` as a candidate
   and coming back as "the threshold" whenever the target accuracy admits every answer — which
   then fails the rule's own `min_confidence` validation when frozen and reused (the exact
   failure the #148 re-review's "one honest residual" and recipe 09's own review documented).
   `_conf_inputs` now passes `unit_interval=True` through to `_floats`, so `selective_curve`,
   `select_confidence_threshold` and `evaluate_selective` all raise `ValueError` on an
   out-of-range confidence, sentinel or otherwise.

2. **`evaluate_outcomes(accepted, correct) -> SelectiveResult`**, the decisions-based
   counterpart `evaluate_selective` is missing. `accepted[i]` is whether the rule answered
   example `i`, as the rule itself decided it (not a reconstruction); `correct[i]` is whether an
   answered example's answer was right. It returns the same `SelectiveResult` shape
   (`n_total`, `n_answered`, `coverage`, `accuracy`, `risk`), with `threshold` NaN — no single
   confidence cut-off produced the split, so a threshold is undefined there, not merely
   unreported, following the module's existing NaN convention. For a rule whose only review
   branch is a confidence gate, `evaluate_outcomes(confidence >= t, correct)` and
   `evaluate_selective(correct, confidence, t)` agree on every other field; this is proven (not
   just argued) on synthetic data across seven thresholds in
   `test_evaluate_outcomes_matches_evaluate_selective_for_a_confidence_only_rule`, and a second
   test shows them diverging once a rule has an unconditional second branch.

`docs/evaluation.md` documents the full convention under "Selective prediction": when
`evaluate_selective` is right, when it silently disagrees with the rule, why the sentinel
construction is fragile (one-directional — it cannot follow a later change to the rule's own
confidence comparison — and can itself be selected as an out-of-range threshold), and
`evaluate_outcomes` as the replacement. `docs/recipe-template.md` qualifies the "`evaluate_selective`
reports the same split" sentence that recipes 01, 05 and 07 (07 after its #148 re-review) carry:
true only when the rule's only review branch is the confidence gate, with `evaluate_outcomes`
named for every other case.

### Why `recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb` is untouched

The issue and my brief both named "the template's sentence" for qualification. I checked the
current `recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb` directly (`json.dumps` of the whole notebook, not a
per-cell grep, to be sure a split source string wasn't hiding it): it does not contain the
sentence "`evaluate_selective` reports the same split", and does not call `evaluate_selective` at
all — its own evaluation section (cell 13) counts what `route` returned with a hand-rolled
`report()` function instead. The sentence exists only in the three recipes that copied it from
an earlier state of this pattern (01, 05, 07), none of which are in this issue's allowed paths
and rule 4 ("do not modify merged recipes") rules them out anyway. I qualified the claim where it
actually lives for future copies: `docs/recipe-template.md`. No notebook re-execution was needed
because no notebook was touched.

## Decisions

- **`evaluate_outcomes` reuses `SelectiveResult` rather than a new dataclass**, with `threshold`
  NaN. This keeps the two functions' results duck-type identical (same fields, same names) so a
  recipe's evaluation cell can treat them interchangeably, and NaN is the module's existing
  convention for "this quantity is undefined here," not merely unknown — a frozen cut-off that
  did not decide the split is exactly that.
- **Named `evaluate_outcomes`, not the issue's suggested `selective_from_outcomes`** (issue
  comment 6072191186's phrasing), to match this module's existing `evaluate_*`/`select_*` family
  (`evaluate_threshold`, `evaluate_selective`, `select_threshold`, `select_confidence_threshold`):
  an `evaluate_*` function that takes the frozen decision and reports on it, with no selection
  step of its own (there is nothing to select: the rule already decided). Recipe 08's own local
  `summarize_outcomes`/`OutcomeSummary` (PR #156, not merged at the time of this branch) is the
  same shape by a different name and without `SelectiveResult` reuse; recipe 08's own PR is the
  right place to decide whether it switches over, not this one.
- **Validation is `unit_interval=True` on the existing `_floats` call, not a new dedicated
  check.** `_noul_array` already uses exactly this parameter for the same purpose; reusing it
  keeps the error message ("`confidence must lie in [0, 1]`") consistent with every other
  range-validated input in the module.
- **No glossary change.** `docs/glossary.md` defines Jev-level terms and this cookbook's
  cross-cutting vocabulary (threshold, provenance, run mode); `evaluate_outcomes` is a function
  name, not a new concept distinct from "threshold" or "coverage/accuracy/risk", which are
  already defined in `docs/evaluation.md`.

## Recipes 07, 08, 09: follow-up, not this branch

Per the issue, recipes are adjusted in their own pull requests:

- **Recipe 09** (PR #153, open at the time of this branch): `placement_confidence`'s `-1.0`
  sentinel for an `unsorted` answer is exactly the construction this issue is about. Its own
  review (comment 6072191186) already found the failure mode this fix closes
  (`select_confidence_threshold` returning `-1.0` as a threshold at `target_accuracy <= 0.9474`).
  Switching its evaluation cell to `evaluate_outcomes` is recipe 09's own follow-up.
- **Recipe 07** (PR #148, merged as `6874762`): already carries a worked-around version of this
  same problem — a `0.0` surrogate confidence fed to `evaluate_selective` for every answer
  `resolve` rejects unconditionally, documented by its own re-review (comment 6072227639) as
  correct for the fixtures it ships but "one-directional" and "the missing piece in
  `jev_cookbook.evaluation`" (which is this issue). It is merged, so this branch does not touch
  it; a follow-up could replace the surrogate-confidence construction with `evaluate_outcomes`.
- **Recipe 08** (PR #156, open at the time of this branch): already built its own
  `OutcomeSummary`/`summarize_outcomes` in `helpers.py` for exactly this reason (its own PR
  description names the gap and says it did not open this issue only because "the brief says the
  orchestrator does that" — issue #155 is that issue). A follow-up to recipe 08's own PR could
  switch to the shared `evaluate_outcomes` instead of the recipe-local helper.

I did not touch any of the three; all are outside this issue's allowed paths, and 07 is merged
(rule: never modify a merged recipe).

## Recipe checklist

Not applicable: this is foundation work, no recipe folder is touched.

- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see below).

## Acceptance criteria (issue #155)

1. **`select_confidence_threshold` validates its inputs: confidences outside `[0, 1]` raise a
   clear `ValueError`, with a test** — met. `_conf_inputs` now validates via
   `unit_interval=True`; `selective_curve` and `evaluate_selective` get the same guard for free
   since they share it. Tests: `test_select_confidence_threshold_rejects_out_of_range_confidence`,
   `test_selective_curve_rejects_out_of_range_confidence`,
   `test_evaluate_selective_rejects_out_of_range_confidence`.
2. **`docs/evaluation.md` documents the convention for rules with an option-based review branch;
   a short, tested helper is acceptable; the template's sentence is qualified** — met. See
   "Selective prediction" in `docs/evaluation.md` and the new bullet in `docs/recipe-template.md`.
   `evaluate_outcomes` is the helper (not "trivial" in the sense of a one-off, but the same size
   and shape as `evaluate_selective`, tested the same way, and exported from the shared module
   rather than left recipe-local).
3. **Recipes 07 and 09 are adjusted in their own pull requests or a follow-up** — not this
   branch's job per the issue; see "Recipes 07, 08, 09" above for what each needs.

## How it was verified

All commands run from the repository root, Linux, no `.env`, no API key, `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE`
unset, default service tier, heavy jobs one at a time under the shared `HEAVY.lock`, in the
foreground:

```
uv venv --python 3.14 .venv && uv pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt
uv venv --python 3.10 .venv310 && uv pip install -e ".[dev]"   -> both installs clean

ruff check .                                   -> All checks passed!
ruff format --check .                          -> 102 files already formatted
ruff format --check docs/evaluation.md docs/recipe-template.md  -> 2 files already formatted
python tools/check_hygiene.py                  -> Hygiene check passed: 142 file(s) scanned.
python tools/render_catalog.py --check         -> exit 0 (README already current; untouched)

# targeted, both interpreters
.venv/bin/python    -m pytest tests/test_evaluation.py tests/test_evaluation_answers.py -q
  -> 138 passed
.venv310/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation.py tests/test_evaluation_answers.py -q
  -> 138 passed

# full suite, 3.14, nice -n 10 timeout 1500, OMP/MKL/OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2, under HEAVY.lock
python -m pytest -q                            -> 1538 passed, 3 skipped in ~82s
  (run twice across this branch's work, identical result both times; the 3 skips are
  typesafe_sdk/pre-commit not installed, pre-existing and unrelated)
```

**Mutation (`timeout 300`, under `HEAVY.lock`):** removed `unit_interval=True` from the
`_conf_inputs` call (the one-line guard this issue asks for) and re-ran the targeted test file:

```
FFF........                                                              [100%]
FAILED tests/test_evaluation.py::test_selective_curve_rejects_out_of_range_confidence
FAILED tests/test_evaluation.py::test_select_confidence_threshold_rejects_out_of_range_confidence
FAILED tests/test_evaluation.py::test_evaluate_selective_rejects_out_of_range_confidence
3 failed, 8 passed, 115 deselected
```

Exactly the three tests that name the guard fail; the file was restored byte-identical
immediately after (`diff` against a saved copy, clean) and the full suite re-run clean
afterwards (1538 passed, 3 skipped).

`recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb` was not touched (see "Why ... is untouched" above), so no
re-execution was needed; `tools/check_notebook_fresh.py` and the notebook-CI logic are exercised
by the full suite's existing `tests/test_notebook_ci_fresh.py` /
`tests/test_notebook_ci_workflows.py`, both passing above.

## New public names

- `jev_cookbook.evaluation.evaluate_outcomes(accepted: Iterable, correct: Iterable) ->
  SelectiveResult` — new function, added to `__all__`.
- No new types: `evaluate_outcomes` returns the existing `SelectiveResult` (its `threshold` field
  is now documented as NaN when the result came from `evaluate_outcomes`).

## Unfinished

Nothing in this branch's own scope. Recipes 07/08/09 switching to `evaluate_outcomes` is
explicitly follow-up work per the issue (see above), not something this PR does.

title: Recipe 10: Answer relevance check
body:
Closes #10

## What this adds

`recipes/10-answer-relevance-check/`: a Level 1 `Noul` recipe that judges whether a candidate
response addresses the user's question the user actually asked, so Python can separate relevant
answers from off-topic replies. One proposition ("This response addresses the question the user
actually asked.") is sent to Jev per (question, response) pair. Python chooses a business
threshold on `validation` with `select_threshold(objective="f1")` and freezes it, chooses a
separate certainty gate with `select_confidence_threshold(..., target_accuracy=1.0)` using
`jev_cookbook.evaluation.noul_confidence` (`|2p - 1|`, S03) and freezes that too, and the rule in
`helpers.check_relevance` produces one of three outcomes: `relevant`, `not_relevant`, or `review`
(an uncertain pair, routed to a simulated `jev_cookbook.simulation.ReviewQueue` the notebook
builds and shows). The evaluation reports precision and recall across the full threshold sweep on
`validation`, then reports once on `test`: `evaluate_threshold` for the business rule alone and
`evaluate_selective` for what the certainty gate actually buys.

### The question

- **Proposition:** "This response addresses the question the user actually asked."
- **State Jev sees:** `{"question": ..., "response": ...}` (the `pair_id` bookkeeping identifier
  stays in Python).
- **Hard cases in the fixtures:** a clearly relevant response, a clearly off-topic response
  (boilerplate, repeats-the-question, deflects, wrong field, unrelated subject), a response that
  only *partly* addresses its question (gold labels deliberately mixed true/false, stored
  probability within 0.09 of an even split), and a fluent, confident-sounding response that
  answers a *different* question from the one asked (`*-hard-wrong`, stored confidently true
  while gold is false).

### Fixtures

48 pairs: 23 `validation`, 23 `test`, 2 `demo` (never scored). 46 labels. Every response is
`synthetic`; none recorded.

### Thresholds and evaluation numbers

- Business threshold (chosen on `validation`, frozen): **0.55** (F1 0.960 on `validation`:
  precision 0.923, recall 1.000).
- Certainty gate (chosen on `validation`, frozen): **0.64**.
- `validation` (selection step, not a reported result): 10 judged relevant (10/10 right among
  those), 5 sent to review, 8 judged not relevant. Review band: `v18`-`v21` (the four genuinely
  ambiguous pairs, stored within 0.09 of an even split, mixed gold) plus `v22-hard-wrong` (0.78,
  excluded because excluding it is exactly what lets this gate reach `target_accuracy=1.0` on
  `validation`, where it is the one wrong business decision).
- `test` (reported once, both thresholds frozen): precision 0.923, recall 1.000, F1 0.960 (business
  rule alone). Selective: coverage 0.826 (19 of 23 ungated), accuracy 0.947, **risk 0.053** (one
  wrong ungated decision: `t22-hard-wrong`, stored at 0.83, whose certainty, 0.66, clears the
  0.64 gate even though the gold label is false — the near-identical `v22-hard-wrong` on
  `validation`, at 0.78/0.56, does not). Review band on `test`: `t18`-`t21` (4 pairs).
- Request count in live mode: **48** (one call per fixture pair, each pair decided once and the
  cached answer reused everywhere it is shown again); README says to raise
  `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` to at least 48 before a live run.

## Decisions

- **Certainty-gate selector:** `select_confidence_threshold(..., target_accuracy=1.0)`, the same
  choice recipes 01/03/04 make for their single confidence threshold, rather than `min_coverage`.
  On this fixture set the two give the same answer (0.64) regardless, because 0.64 is both the
  lowest threshold reaching 100% accuracy and the one `select_confidence_threshold`'s
  tie-break (toward more coverage) would pick under `min_coverage` too.
- **A real interaction worth flagging for later recipes:** because `target_accuracy=1.0` forces
  the gate to exclude `validation`'s own single wrong business decision, this recipe's up-close
  demo of `v22-hard-wrong` reaches `review`, not a confidently-wrong `relevant` — the general
  "certainty can't distinguish confidently wrong from confidently right" property is instead
  pinned in `tests/test_helpers.py` with an isolated, far-from-any-chosen-threshold example
  (`noul=0.95`), and demonstrated end to end by `test`'s near-identical `t22-hard-wrong`, which
  *does* clear the frozen gate and is what makes `risk` non-zero. The notebook's prose says this
  explicitly rather than asserting the wrong thing about `v22-hard-wrong`'s own outcome.
- **ReviewQueue holds only the `review` outcome.** Unlike recipe 02 (where both the acted-on and
  the reviewed outcome share a workflow queue), a `relevant` response here is simply shown to the
  user and a `not_relevant` one is suppressed — neither needs a person, so only `review` items are
  queued.
- **Selective metrics read `check_relevance`'s own `is_relevant` field**, never a re-derived
  `noul >= threshold`, per the #148/#155 convention.
- **Next-step links:** `02-refund-intent-detection` (same three-path `Noul` pattern) and
  `08-faq-selection` (a `Choice` question over the same kind of candidate-response search), both
  in the `Search & retrieval` category with this recipe.

## Commands run (actual results)

```
python tools/new_recipe.py 10                                   # scaffolded
python recipes/10-answer-relevance-check/build_fixtures.py      # wrote 48 examples, 46 labels, 48 responses
python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/10-answer-relevance-check
  -> recipes/10-answer-relevance-check: fixtures valid (mode replay)
pytest recipes/10-answer-relevance-check                        # 24 passed (Python 3.14 venv)
pytest recipes/10-answer-relevance-check                        # 24 passed (Python 3.10 venv)

title: Recipe 06: Multiple topic labels
body:
Closes #6

## What this adds

`recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels/`: tag customer feedback with every applicable topic from a
fixed list of five labels (`pricing`, `reliability`, `usability`, `support`, `feature_request`),
using one independent `Noul` proposition per label, all five sent together in a single request
because they describe the same state (S02).

- `helpers.py`: `LABELS` (the fixed label list, built into five `Noul` questions by a single
  Python loop), `build_state`/`build_questions`, and `decide_tags` — the three-path rule: a
  per-label business tag (`noul >= threshold`) gated by one shared confidence cutoff built from
  `|2p - 1|` (S03); a label below the cutoff is marked `uncertain` and goes to review instead of
  being reported either way, whatever the business tag says. `tag_set`/`uncertain_labels` read
  the rule's output.
- `build_fixtures.py`: 40 examples (19 `validation`, 19 `test`, 2 `demo`), each with a gold label
  *set* (zero, one, or up to four of the five labels) and five hand-written probabilities. Hard
  cases: two "literal reading" (S07, item 1) lookalikes (`v09-lookalike`/`t16-lookalike-wrong`,
  text that uses a label-associated word — "price", "feature" — without raising that topic),
  `t16-lookalike-wrong` wrong *and* confident on `test`; five low-confidence crossover pairs on
  `validation` (one per label) that the confidence cutoff is chosen to catch; a 4-label and a
  0-label example in both `validation` and `test`.
- The notebook: per-label thresholds via `select_threshold("f1")` on `validation`, frozen before
  `test`; one confidence cutoff via `select_confidence_threshold`, chosen by pooling all 95
  (example, label) validation pairs (reasoning in "Python's part": 19 examples is too few to
  trust a second parameter per label, and every label's confidence sits on the same 0-1 scale per
  S03, so pooling is valid); a `jev_cookbook.simulation.ReviewQueue` built and shown with every
  flagged (example, label) pair; evaluation via `multilabel_from_noul`/`multilabel_metrics`/
  `exact_set_match` for the tag set, and the confidence gate's own coverage/accuracy/risk counted
  directly from `decide_tags`'s outcomes (not `evaluate_selective`, which is written for a plain
  answer-or-abstain rule, not one layered on five per-label thresholds).
- `tests/test_helpers.py` (28 tests, parametrized over every label): the three outcomes for every
  label, both threshold boundaries inclusive, invalid threshold/cutoff ranges, empty/full tag
  sets, state hiding the identifier, and the replay-key-matches-the-question check.
  `tests/test_build_fixtures.py`: the template's three guard tests (refusal to overwrite a
  recorded `responses.json`, `--force` restoring it, byte-identical `_dump` output), shipped per
  the current brief guidance pending #137.

## Decisions a later builder should know about

- **Per-label business thresholds, one shared confidence cutoff.** The issue's build note says
  Python applies a per-label threshold, so each of the five gets its own `select_threshold`.
  Pooling the confidence cutoff instead of selecting it per label is a deliberate choice: with
  only 19 validation examples, a single label's own subset (19 pairs) is too small to trust a
  second selected parameter; pooled, it is 95.
- **The confidence gate's selective numbers are computed from `decide_tags`'s own outcomes**, via
  a small `tally_outcomes` helper in the notebook, not from `jev_cookbook.evaluation
  .evaluate_selective`. That helper is written for a plain "answer or abstain" rule; a per-label
  threshold plus a shared confidence gate is not the same split it was designed to describe, and
  the recipe says so in "Evaluation" rather than claiming otherwise (per the brief guidance from
  the #148 review).
- **Up-close examples are `demo` or `validation` only** (`d02-none`, `v09-lookalike`,
  `d01-mixed3`), never `test`, per the same guidance.
- **`feature_request`'s threshold lands high (0.82)** specifically because of
  `v16-lookalike-wrong` (validation) and its `test` twin `t16-lookalike-wrong`: a lower threshold
  would catch the genuine feature requests but also tag the lookalike, so `select_threshold`
  trades a little recall (missing `v05`, a genuinely low-confidence feature request) for
  precision. This is a real, inspectable trade-off from the fixture data, not a hand-tuned number.
- **Gap/failure this recipe's fixtures could not avoid:** at `target_accuracy=0.97` the review
  queue holds 6 items on `validation` and 0 on `test` (`test`'s only wrong pair, the
  lookalike-wrong one, is confidently wrong, which is exactly the point: a cutoff chosen on a
  handful of ambiguous `validation` pairs is a guarantee about those pairs, not about a confident
  mistake elsewhere). The notebook's "Evaluation" section discusses this directly rather than
  leaving the empty `test` queue unexplained.
- No shared-package gap was hit: `multilabel_from_noul`, `multilabel_metrics`, `exact_set_match`
  and `noul_confidence` all worked exactly as `docs/evaluation.md` documents them, including for
  a five-label recipe.

## Request budget

Each of the 40 fixture examples needs exactly one request (all five labels' propositions share
one state and go together, per S02), so this notebook makes 40 requests, not 200 — 200 is the
number of individual yes/no *decisions* inside those 40 requests (40 examples × 5 labels). 40
exceeds the live backend's default budget of 25, so the README's "Switch to live" section tells
the reader to set `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=40` or higher first.

## How it was verified

All commands below were run from a clean worktree off `main` at `3004c0f`, Python 3.14
(`.venv`, `pip install -e ".[dev,ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`) unless noted,
under the shared heavy-job slot for the notebook executions and the full suite.

- `python recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels/build_fixtures.py` — wrote 40 examples, 38 labels, 40
  responses; byte-identical between a Python 3.14 (`.venv`) and a Python 3.10 (`.venv310`,
  `.[dev]`) run of the same script, on `inputs.jsonl`, `labels.jsonl` and `responses.json`.
- `python -m jev_cookbook.fixtures validate recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels` — `fixtures valid
  (mode replay)`.
- `pytest recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels` — 28 passed, on both Python 3.14 and Python 3.10.
- `python tools/execute_notebook.py recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels`, run twice in a row under
  the slot — byte-identical both times (`diff -q` empty); outputs committed.
- `ruff check .` — All checks passed.
- `ruff format --check .` — 96 files already formatted.
- `python tools/check_hygiene.py` — Hygiene check passed: 133 file(s) scanned. (One fixture's
  feedback text originally used the word "agent", which is this shared container's own account
  name; the hygiene scanner's local-username rule flagged the printed notebook output as a
  coincidental match, not a real leak. Reworded that one fixture's text — "the rep fixed my
  issue" — rather than weakening the check.)
- `python tools/check_recipe_scope.py --base origin/main --head <commit> --branch
  recipe/06-multiple-topic-labels --body-file <this description>` — `scope ok: recipe pull
  request for #6 (06-multiple-topic-labels): 9 changed paths`.
- `grep -rn TODO recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels` — empty.
- Full suite, foreground, under the slot: `OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 MKL_NUM_THREADS=2
  OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2 nice -n 10 timeout 1500 python -m pytest -q` — 1506 passed, 3 skipped in
  84.24s.
- `python tools/render_catalog.py` was **not** run, as instructed; `Catalog (README is current)`
  is expected to be red until the integration worker regenerates the root README in this PR.

### Evaluation numbers (synthetic fixtures; pipeline checks, not Jev results)

Per-label thresholds (chosen on `validation`, frozen): `pricing` 0.44, `reliability` 0.47,
`usability` 0.52, `support` 0.40, `feature_request` 0.82. Confidence cutoff (pooled over 95
validation pairs, `target_accuracy=0.97`): 0.12.

`test` (19 examples, 95 (example, label) pairs), business rule only:

| label | precision | recall | f1 | support |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| pricing | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 7 |
| reliability | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 5 |
| usability | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 5 |
| support | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 5 |
| feature_request | 0.667 | 0.667 | 0.667 | 3 |

micro precision/recall/f1 0.960/0.960/0.960; macro 0.933/0.933/0.933; exact label-set match
0.895.

Confidence-gate selective numbers, counted from `decide_tags`'s own outcomes: `validation`
answered 89 of 95 (coverage 0.9368), accuracy 0.9888, risk 0.0112; `test` answered 95 of 95
(coverage 1.0000), accuracy 0.9789, **risk 0.0211** (from `t16-lookalike-wrong`'s confident, wrong
`feature_request` tag, which the gate was never built to catch).

## Recipe checklist

- [x] Changes are confined to `recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels/`, plus the generated README
  regions regenerated by the integration worker (nothing else outside the recipe folder)
- [ ] README regenerated with `python tools/render_catalog.py` — not applicable to this PR; the
  integration worker does this, per CONTRIBUTING.md's generated-README exception
- [x] `git diff --raw -M origin/main...HEAD` lists only `recipes/06-multiple-topic-labels/`
  paths, every mode `100644`, no symlink/mode/type change, no rename or deletion out of scope
  (verified with `tools/check_recipe_scope.py`, which also covers the `README.md` content rule)
- [x] Notebook runs top to bottom offline, with no key and no network
- [x] Live path is opt-in and uses the same question definitions
- [x] Every response fixture records its provenance (`synthetic`); the notebook states which
  mode it ran in (`run_header`, first output)
- [x] No claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost without recorded live inference
- [x] Fixtures are synthetic, include the hard cases (no-label, 3+/4-label, two literal-reading
  lookalikes, a confidently-wrong test case), and carry gold label sets
- [x] Python owns every side effect; actions are simulated (`ReviewQueue`, nothing executed)
- [x] Evaluation against gold labels, with `jev_cookbook.evaluation`; the issue names no baseline
- [x] Every acceptance criterion on the issue is met (see the issue's checklist; all nine items
  addressed — notebook runs offline with committed outputs, live path opt-in and same questions,
  fixtures synthetic with hard cases and gold labels and pass the validator, every response
  fixture's provenance recorded and the notebook states its mode, per-label precision/recall and
  micro/macro F1 and exact-set match reported, every term explained on first appearance, three
  individual typed answers (fifteen, across three examples) shown and discussed before any
  aggregate, no claim about Jev's real quality without recorded inference, README states what it
  teaches/how to run it/what was and was not measured, PR confined to the recipe folder)
